News.title: Brit, 33, becomes first UK national to die fighting for Putin after being hit by Ukrainian suicide drone on frontline
News.content:
A SOLDIER who betrayed his country to fight for Putin has become the first Brit to die fighting for Russia.

Bradley Townsend, from Yorkshire, was killed after being struck by a Ukrainian suicide bomb on the frontline.

He reportedly died in June while fighting for Mad Vlad’s army.



The British Government have said that they are aware of reports of his death and are “in contact with his family”.



Enlisting with the Russian army “could be breaking UK laws”, the government warned.

News.title: Man, 33, charged after couple ‘caught having sex’ on Ferris wheel at Download Festival in front of thousands
News.content:
ROMP CHARGE Man, 33, charged after couple ‘caught having sex’ on Ferris wheel at Download Festival in front of thousands

A 33-YEAR-OLD man has been charged with outraging public decency after a couple was caught allegedly having sex on a Ferris wheel in front of thousands of revellers.

Leicestershire Police launched a probe into the incident after the pair were filmed reportedly engaging in sexual acts at Download Festival in June.



Fans were waiting to see Guns ‘n’ Roses play at the festival in Castle Donington, Leicestershire, when they spotted the couple.

The duo were seen, apparently engaged in sexual activity, in one of the cabins of the ferris wheel as it rotated.



Images and video of the indecent act was shared widely on social media at the time.

Police were alerted to the incident and launched a probe into the alleged public romp.



Following enquiries cops confirmed they had charged Innes Miller, 33, of Edwalton, Nottinghamshire, with outraging public decency.

The force says a woman has already been identified and voluntarily interviewed as part of their enquiries.

Miller is now due to appear at Leicester Magistrates’ Court on September 10.

When the couple were spotted romping on the ferris wheel, a stunned witness told The Sun: “Originally for the first rotation of the wheel people thought he was just standing behind her with his arms around her, looking at the view.



“But, as it got lower, somebody shouted ‘I can see her pants pulled aside!’”

Download Festival is the biggest rock and metal event in the UK and is attended by 80,000 every year.

But, the witness, who is a regular festival attendee, said: “I have never seen anything like this.

“They were literally in a glass pod above everyone’s heads at the busiest point of the night, just before Guns ‘n Roses were due on.

“It sort of brought everyone together in a weird way, before they were spotted the atmosphere was nervous apprehension because they’re always late on.



“As soon as the cameras came out and word started getting around about what happened the atmosphere completely changed – they made the night.

“All I can think is they thought the glass was tinted, but it wasn’t at all, it was actually spotless, you could see everything.”

News.title: Putin unleashes new nuclear sub able to carry ‘doomsday’ torpedos for first time in chilling warning to the West
News.content:
VLADIMIR Putin’s “doomsday” sub loaded with nuclear torpedoes has been unleashed for the first time in a chilling warning to the west.

The deadly Khabarovsk carries up to six Poseidon nukes and can blast underwater bombs so powerful they create tsunamis.



The 10,000 ton sub quietly slipped into the White Sea to commence a series of chilling weapons trials last week.

Poseidon missiles have a range of more than 6,000 miles and can dive to depths of 3,280ft.



British sub-sea oil and gas pipelines run at depths of 3,000ft.

And experts claim that underwater explosions from Poseidon bombs could trigger massive surges of Tsunami-style waves onto British shores.

It comes as prime minister Andy Burnham renewed Britain’s pledge to aid Ukraine – and promised to send more British drones into battle.

The move has enraged Putin and his cronies, with state TV presenter Vladimir Solovyov threatening: “Give the British three days to learn to breathe underwater, then hit them with Poseidon.”

Ominously, the Russian embassy warned that the more Britain helped Ukraine, “the higher the price it will pay”.

Burnham has ignored the warning and insisted that Britain is not a “fairweather friend”.



Last year, Putin boasted that his Poseidon missiles were unbeatable, saying “there is no way to intercept it”.

The incredible claim has not been independently verified.

The missiles – named after the powerful Greek god of the sea – were first developed in 2002.



Former president Dmitry Medvedev dubbed them a true “doomsday weapon” with Russian journalists claiming they could “drown Britain”.

Though the claims remain unproven, analysts point out that the devastation could still be significant.

Coastal cities could be decimated and water and land contaminated.

Military expert Dr Richard Connolly told the Telegraph that Mad Vlad was merely using the Poseidon sub for propaganda – and had no intention of striking Britian.

“If they were to do what the Russian TV presenters are proposing, they’d face retaliation from Britain’s Trident nuclear deterrent”, Connolly explained.



“So they wouldn’t do it, because they know they’d pay a price”, he reasoned.

The analyst, who is an associate fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (Rusi) military think tank, calls the Poseidon missiles a “boutique” weapon because they are only produced in small numbers.

Nonetheless, the threat posed by the nuclear warheads may be enough to spur big spending from NATO.

“We’re in a very dangerous position at the moment,” says Connolly. “We may disagree with Russia and its security architecture. But it’s a different thing to say you’ve got to just keep escalating.

“You’d be spending an enormous amount of money to counter something that will only be used when you’re already in a nuclear war,” he pointed out.

“And, you know – it’s not like we’ll be around anyway.”

News.title: M9 wrong-way crash teen brought to church in horse-drawn carriage for funeral as priest says ‘families changed forever’
News.content:
THERE was a heavy police presence at the funeral mass of the fourth teenager killed in a wrong-way crash on the M9 last week.

Jeremy O’Brien, 18, died after the BMW he was travelling in drove down the wrong side of the M9 in Kildare and ploughed into a family driving to Dublin Airport at 3am.



He was pronounced dead at the scene of the horror M9 crash alongside Joey Carthy, 15, Alex McCarthy, 16, Jack Kennedy and Kamil Pustkowski, both aged 17.

Sisters Niamh and Alma Kinsella, 30s, younger sister Ella Hendricken, 20s, and Alma’s seven-year-old son Yemi all remain in hospital with serious injuries after their car was hit by the teens’ BMW.



Garda checkpoints and various garda vehicles, including the Public Order Unit, were all in place in Carlow town ahead of Jeremy O’Brien’s funeral mass at 11am today.

Armed garda detectives were also stationed at garda checkpoints on the roads leading to The Holy Family Church in Askea.



Inside the church Jeremy’s remains lay in a plain brown coffin as Father Tom Little asked the congregation to pray for the innocent family “fighting to recover” in hospital.

The parish priest said in a funeral homily that there are “no words to express” the “sadness and loss” across the community after last week’s fatal crash.

The priest also addressed teens’ “wrong” actions in the speech but urged mourners not to let tragedy “become the whole story”.



Father Little told the funeral mass: “Today, as we gather with a deep sense of sadness and loss, we pray for those who have been injured and mourn those who have died.

“The death of a young person is always difficult to accept. There is something especially sad about a young life being taken suddenly, unexpectedly, and before so many hopes and dreams have been realised.

“Today, our grief and sadness is made even heavier because this was an accident that affected not just one person alone. Several lives have been lost, and others have been seriously injured.

“Families have been changed forever. There are people in hospital fighting to recover, and there are families who are beginning the painful journey of learning to live with an empty place at their table.

“At times like this we are left with no words to express our sadness and loss.”



He continued: “We believe that God who gave us life does not abandon us in death. We entrust our loved ones who have gone before us into the merciful hand of God, acknowledging that what the boys did was wrong.

“But we must not allow tragedy to become the whole story as we pray for those who were injured and those who have died.

“So, today, we give thanks for the gift of life, however short it may have been. We give thanks for the love shared, for the memories created, and for the way their lives touched ours.”

Young men attending the service this morning wore T-shirts with a picture of O’Brien emblazoned on the front.

A horse-drawn carriage also arrived at the church to carry the coffin following the funeral mass.



Jeremy O’Brien will be laid to rest at a graveyard in Co Carlow.

The 18-year-old leaves behind his mother Margret, four brothers, grandparents and extended family.

Speaking to The Irish Sun on Sunday ahead of today’s funeral Margret told us: “I am not proud of what happened and I don’t condone what they did

— I wish my son had never got into that car.”

The grieving mother added: “I don’t know if my son was driving the car that night and they made a catastrophic decision to drive down the motorway in the wrong direction.

“I raised my son on my own and I’ve now lost a part of me for life, and so have the other mothers.



“I also don’t know why they drove in that manner and I pray that the full investigation can establish the facts and tell us the truth about what happened.”

Margret also apologised to the three sisters and child injured in the motorway crash that killed her son.

She said: “My heart goes out to this poor family and if I could see them I would apologise.

“I have said prayers for them and I hope to God that they can heal.”

The funeral mass for fellow crash victim Joe Carthy, 15, took place in Athy, Kildare on Friday morning.



A large garda presence was also visible in the town as the teenager’s gold coffin was brought to the church by a horse-drawn carriage.

The remains of Kamil Pustkowski, 17, were brought to a crematorium that same day, after a low-key memorial in Limerick city with just close family and friends.

And the funeral for the third teenager took place on Friday afternoon at the Holy Family Church in Carlow, the same place Jeremy O’Brien’s funeral was held this morning.

Alex McCarthy’s flashy blue coffin arrived to the church on Friday, carried by an elaborate white horse-drawn carriage.

Speaking during McCarthy’s funeral mass Father Tom Little said the grief and heartache caused by the M9 crash was “difficult to put into words”.



He told the mass: “These types of accidents bring a deep sense of shock, anger, questions, regret, and even a sense of disbelief.

“Words cannot express the true feelings of our heart, so today is a day for compassion, prayer, and remembrance.”

The final crash victim, 17-year-old Jack Kennedy, will be remembered during a funeral mass at St Michael’s Parish Church in Athy at 11am tomorrow.

A garda presence at all five funerals was confirmed last week over fears of stunt driving processions or public order incidents at the ceremonies.

A source explained: “There won’t be a completely overt presence, but if you have a situation where young lads begin driving recklessly and doing wheelies or anything of the sort, there are resources in place to deal with that, which include the public order unit.”



RECOMMENDED STORIES

A vigil for the sisters injured in the August 16 crash was held at St Clare’s Church in Graiguecullen on Friday evening, just hours after funerals for three of the wrong-way drivers that hit them.

A GoFundMe set up for the sisters by a friend has raised over €739,000 in just six days.

News.title: Will Meghan Markle star in The Gentlemen? What we know about return to acting as she returns to UK with Harry
News.content:
MEGHAN Markle’s long-awaited acting comeback has been the subject of much speculation, with a role in Guy Ritchie’s Netflix smash The Gentlemen understood to be worth more than £1million.

The Duchess of Sussex is returning to Britain with Prince Harry and their children, but whether she will appear in the gangster comedy-drama is another story altogether.



Will Meghan Markle be in The Gentlemen?

On August 21, The Sun exclusively revealed that Meghan Markle, 45, was in advanced talks for a role in The Gentlemen.

An insider said: “The gossip in TV circles is that Meghan could play the ultimate temptress, who puts the cat among the pigeons by seducing an aristocrat.”



A source said she would be getting “at least £1million” for the part, “perhaps even more”.

But Royal author Tina Brown then claimed the potential deal had collapsed, posting on X: “I learned this morning the casting of Meghan in The Gentlemen has been withdrawn.

“The backlash in the UK was so intense, it became untenable. This does not bode well for Meghan’s acting comeback in the UK.”

Then, on August 23, an insider said that discussions were in fact continuing, with Netflix bosses keen to land the comeback even though nothing formal has been signed.

A TV source said: “Her return to acting is expected to draw a large audience of both her supporters and critics, and is likely to make a lot of money. It will be seen as a major coup for whoever signs her.”

Talent manager Professor Jonathan Shalit, chairman of InterTalent Rights Group, told The Sun on Sunday: “It’s a great show and people love it all over the world. If they sign her, it’s a great signing.”



Netflix is expected to announce a third series later this week.

When is The Gentlemen season 2 on Netflix?

Series 2 of The Gentlemen lands on Netflix on September 3, with all eight episodes dropping at once.

A London premiere is being held the night before, with fans excited that Meghan could potentially be attending as she and Harry are expected to be in the UK.

The Gentlemen is predominantly filmed at the Badminton estate in Gloucestershire, just seven miles from the King’s Highgrove Estate.

Why are Harry and Meghan moving back to the UK?

In a world exclusive, The Sun revealed that the Sussexes have found a new home in the UK.



Harry and Meghan are relocating for “an extended period” after six years in California.

Sources in the US told The Sun that she and Harry secretly told friends that they will return to the UK, while keeping their home in Montecito, California fully staffed.

The source said: “They will return to California in the long term but are moving to the UK to be closer to Charles while he copes with cancer, and because Meghan has secured this secret role.”

Archie, 7, and Lilibet, 5, are expected to start school in Britain in September.

The ongoing talks about her role in The Gentlemen are understood to be one factor behind the move.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Meghan has not taken a scripted role since leaving Suits in 2017.

In 2022, she told Variety: “I’m done. I guess never say never, but my intention is to absolutely not.”

News.title: Comical moment car sent spinning out of control by crash ends up perfectly parked in garage between two vehicles
News.content:
THIS is the wild moment a car careens across the street after crashing into another vehicle before executing a perfect forward bay park.

CCTV footage from the crash shows the grey Ford spiralling out of control in Sao Paulo, Brazil before miraculously slotting between two display cars.



Driver Ana Beatriz Ferreira Godoy, 25, had been cruising along Rua Antonio Alves on Tuesday when her car was suddenly struck.

Another driver had run a stop sign – and ploughed directly into Ana’s Ford Ka.



The two cars collided in a dramatic crossing crash – with one driver appearing to zoom off undamaged.

But Ana’s car was completely knocked off course and rotated 90 degrees to face the Sergipano Veiculos car dealership.



Dramatic footage shows the Grey ford skidding into the entrance of the garage and hitting the red and yellow sales sign.

Miraculously the car then smoothly slots between two other parked vehicles.

Neither of the two display models had so much as a scratch on them.

Concerned staff rushed to the car as the shaken woman clambers out of the vehicle.



Ana, a gamer and telecoms analysts, later joked: “I can’t even parallel park”.

In a supernatural twist, the driver claims she escaped unharmed because of a dream she had three months earlier.

Ana recalled a nightmare about this incident in which she lost control of her car and could not stop.



“Three months ago, I dreamt about an accident where I completely lost control of the car”, she recounted, adding “in the dream, I was very nervous because I couldn’t brake.

“At the moment of the crash, the dream just came back to me, and that is what made me remember to brake”.

People viewing the clip online joked: “Next time, dream about winning the lottery”.

One admired the woman’s driving skills, commending the fact that she “held the steering wheel and didn’t spin”.

Both Ana and the other driver, also a woman, escaped unharmed.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

The reckless motorist has been in touch with Ana to offer money for the crash and damage to her car.

Ana Beatriz’s Ford Ka suffered damage to its axle, bumper, and one of its taillights.

News.title: Drummer, 56, dies mid-performance after collapsing over kit onstage at rock festival in front of horrified fans
News.content:
A DRUMMER has tragically died onstage after collapsing as he and his band performed for a packed out festival crowd.

Malaysian drummer, Raja Azreen Raja Talib fell unconscious while on stage after performing only two songs with his rock band Meditasi.



During the second song of their set, frontman Bakaruddin Daud – also known as Burn – noticed the 56-year-old drummer slump over on his drum kit.

Burn said Raja’s body “was already cold“, when he spoke with Malaysian newspaper Berita Harian.



He said: “I rushed towards him, but I could feel that he was gone,

“I called and patted [him], but there was no response.”

He added that Raja showed no signs of being ill before he went on stage at the Teruntum Rock Festival in Malaysia.

Burn later revealed that the late drummer had recently been diagnosed with diabetes.



After Raja collapsed, he was rushed to Tengku Ampuan Afzan Hospital and given respiratory assistance.

Unfortunately, he was pronounced dead due to heart complications.

Burn said that he was “deeply affected” by Raja’s death, as they had known each other for decades.

Burn handled all of the funeral arrangements, according to Raja’s brother, Azman.

Azman shared that the drummer was hospitalised in June due to heart issues.



He said: “He was hospitalised twice; the first stay lasted two to three weeks before he was admitted again.

“It is possible that extreme fatigue took a toll [on his heart],

He added that Raja “went straight” from a BMX competition to performing at the music festival.

Raja was very passionate about sport and had continued to compete in events after his health had improved.

Meditasi, which means Meditation in Malay, was active in the 1980s and 1990s and disbanded before reuniting in 2015.



The band has more than 46,000 monthly listeners on Spotify.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

As for the future of the band, Burn told the newspaper that he and Meditasi’s guitarist, Rosli Ahmad, have not yet discussed it.

He confirmed, however, that the group will continue to perform as they believe Raja Azreen would have wished.

News.title: Four kids found in deplorable conditions left with ‘unnatural’ walk after being ‘confined to tractor trailer for YEARS’
News.content:
'CURLED UP SIDE BY SIDE' Four kids found in deplorable conditions left with ‘unnatural’ walk after being ‘confined to tractor trailer for YEARS’

FOUR children were allegedly confined to the cab of a tractor-trailer for nearly seven years – leaving them with an “unnatural” walk, cops say.

The kids were reportedly forced to sleep curled up together in a tiny bunk and were deprived of schooling, medical care and even regular access to showers and a bathroom.



Florida couple Keisha Epps, 51, and her fiancé Tamra Marshon Stewart, 37, have now been charged with child neglect over the alleged horror conditions.

The children had reportedly been living inside the truck’s cab with the couple since December 2019 as Epps worked as a truck driver on a route between Miami and Atlanta.



They were allegedly kept inside the vehicle “for the majority of their days,” according to court documents.



Investigators claim the confinement had taken such a toll that a detective noticed the children were “walking with an unnatural gait from being confined to the cab.”

The four kids allegedly shared a single bunk where they had to lie “curled up side by side because they could not fit.”

They also claimed they were not given enough time to shower, use the restroom or exercise outside the truck.

And the children told interviewers at a child advocacy center they “have not been allowed to attend school for approximately five years,” Fox News reported.



Investigators said the youngsters were “fed poorly” and allegedly received no medical or dental care – even when they were injured.

One child recalled suffering a serious burn from cooked noodles while living in the truck.

“There was a lot of blood,” she told investigators.

The child claimed neither Epps nor Stewart sought medical treatment for the injury, which allegedly left her with a “permanent scar”.

More disturbing allegations emerged when the children were interviewed by investigators.



They reportedly claimed they witnessed sexual abuse and confronted Stewart about it.

Stewart then allegedly “beat them by punching them in their heads,” according to the reports.

The identity of the alleged sexual abuse victim was unclear in the heavily redacted court documents.

The children also claimed they told Epps about the alleged abuse and that she had witnessed it herself.

Investigators allege Epps called one of the children “derogatory names and continued to leave them alone with” Stewart.



One of the four children was also reportedly discovered to have an untreated sexually transmitted infection.

The reports do not disclose the children’s ages, sexes, relationships to one another or their relationships to Epps and Stewart.

Stewart allegedly watched the youngsters while Epps was driving, sleeping or showering.

Epps and Stewart were both arrested on August 6 following the investigation by the Jacksonville Sheriff’s Office.

Each has been charged with four counts of child neglect – one for each child.



Investigators alleged their actions amounted to a “committed, willful failure or omission to provide a child with the care, supervision, and services necessary to maintain the child’s physical and mental health, including but not limited to, food, nutrition, clothing, shelter, supervision, medicine and medical services that a prudent person would consider essential to the wellbeing of the child.”

Each child neglect count is a third-degree felony carrying a possible sentence of up to five years behind bars, as well as up to five years of probation and a fine of up to $5,000.

Court documents also state that “capital sexual battery charges” against Stewart will be filed in Florida’s 9th Judicial District by the Statewide Prosecutor.

Under Florida law, a person convicted of sexual battery against a child younger than 12 can face life in prison without parole or the death penalty.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Epps and Stewart remain behind bars in the Duval County Jail awaiting trial.



Epps’ bond was set at $400,012, while Stewart was being held without bond.

News.title: Social media firms should remove dangerous driving videos, minister says
News.content:
Pollard said the government had "already taken steps" to tell social media companies to take down such content.

He added: "They know exactly what content is on their site, they know how their algorithm works.

"They also know that people post content to get views and the more views you get, sometimes you get money for it, so it's a financial incentive to post outrageous content that gets more people watching it."

A Downing Street spokeswoman said "the glorification of dangerous driving for clips and entertainment is utterly disgraceful".

She added that the culture secretary has been clear that footage should be removed by social media platforms "in line with their legal obligations", and that Ofcom has the government's "full backing to take action" against those that fail in their duties.

Video content featuring illegal activity is not necessarily illegal itself - according to the Online Safety Act - it is up to the social network to decide whether flagged content is illegal and act accordingly.

TikTok said its policies prohibit content that could cause significant physical harm, including dangerous driving.

It added that it is actively removing videos and accounts that break its rules, including the account believed to belong to Saddington.

The company said between January and March 2026, 99.8% of the content removed for violating those policies it took down proactively.

While TikTok is taking some videos down, it is not necessarily because it has deemed them to be illegal - it may only be because they breach the firm's own terms and conditions.

There are specific exceptions which are set out in the Online Safety Act, but they can be difficult to interpret.

For example, content showing someone being killed is not necessarily illegal unless it is being shared by a terrorist group, and/or accessible to children.

The BBC has also contacted Meta and X for comment.

News.title: Divorce, smartphones and control - BBC sees how Taliban run Afghanistan
News.content:
Governor Abdullah Sarhadi gives money to treat a boy's broken arm and hands out funds for a local mosque - then, in his office in northern Afghanistan, an astonishing exchange unfolds.

A young woman tells the grey-bearded former Taliban commander that she wants to divorce her husband, who she accuses of months of abuse and beatings.

She will not take no for an answer.

In a country where girls are banned from secondary education, the 18-year-old argues her case calmly and confidently, her face completely hidden behind a full-face veil and sunglasses.

"If there was any chance to live together, I wouldn't be hereâ¦ I have taken my decision," she says.

After trying to persuade her to avoid divorce, the governor later comments that women are "mindless" and "deficient in intellect", to laughter from the male officials, bodyguards and elders around him.

The moment gives a rare glimpse into the day-to-day realities of the Taliban's rule, five years after they swept aside the US-backed government in 2021.

News.title: Graduate job vacancies drop by almost 50% in a year, survey suggests
News.content:
The number of graduate jobs has fallen almost in half in the past year, according to new figures, as employers cut entry-level roles in favour of AI and battle rising costs.

Jobs website Adzuna said it had just 8,383 graduate vacancies listed in July, down from 15,397 at the same point last year.

Adzuna also found competition among job seekers across all levels is rising, with an average of 2.14 job seekers per vacancy in July, up from 1.93 a year earlier.

Businesses have said employer national insurance and minimum wage hikes have made hiring more expensive, particularly for junior staff.

The number of graduate vacancies listed hit its lowest level since Adzuna started recording such data in 2016. The firm pointed to a peak for graduate roles in 2017, when it had more than 55,800 listed on its website. That is more than six times the number of roles listed on the site in July.

Andrew Hunter, the co-founder of Adzuna, said the figures show "employers still haven't found a reason to open up hiring" for recent graduates.

Official figures show the UK's youth unemployment rate - which covers 16-to-24-year-olds - was 16.2% in the three months to March 2026. The number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) is now over one million.

Young people have told BBC News previously they have applied for hundreds of jobs before even receiving a response.

They also expressed frustration at the growing number of employers using AI to screen applications.

Many university graduates also face mounting student debt.

Former government minister Alan Milburn is leading a major review of the youth unemployment crisis. He has previously said the number of entry-level jobs is shrinking, as is the number of part-time jobs traditionally filled by teenagers and students.

The Adzuna data also showed vacancies for jobs in travel, teaching and construction rose in recent weeks.

But sectors including healthcare, nursing, hospitality and logistics posted fewer vacancies.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham recently changed the rules for public contracts so that companies bidding for them have to show how they will create jobs and training opportunities.

News.title: 'It's not Alton Towers' - rows break out over queuing at Wales' highest mountain
News.content:
Visitors to Wales' highest mountain are being urged to respect others by not skipping queues to reach the top following rows among climbers.

Recent hot weather means there have been bumper summer crowds at Yr Wyddfa, also known as Snowdon, where people have reportedly waited more than one hour to reach the 1,085m (3,560ft)-high summit.

Social media videos have shown arguments among queue-jumpers and those patiently waiting their turn to touch the metal plate that marks the top.

A recent video showed Marc Screeton, from Manchester, being heckled as he bypassed the line, saying: "Imagine queuing on a mountain? No chance."

But others have said queuing is necessary for safety reasons.

News.title: Race Across the World star Jo Gardiner dies aged 61 one year after son's death
News.content:
A former Race Across the World contestant has died, a year after her son and co-star's death in a car crash.

Jo Gardiner, 61, died "following a long and courageous battle with cancer", her family said.

Gardiner, a physiotherapist from Manchester, travelled across South America with her son Sam in the second series of the BBC show, which aired in 2020.

Her family said she was "one of a kind" who "lived fully, fiercely and never did anything by halves".

News.title: Mother, grandmother and stepfather sentenced for 'house of terror' abuse
News.content:
A mother, grandmother and stepfather who subjected three children to years of abuse in a "house of terror" have avoided jail.

Shirley Freeman, Julia Stephen and David McColl's victims were beaten, starved and psychologically tormented between 2003 and 2012.

Freeman, 51, and Stephen, 69, were earlier found guilty of cruel and unnatural treatment. McColl, 50, admitted the crimes.

At Aberdeen Sheriff Court, Sheriff Craig Findlater said no sentence could "repair the awful childhoods" of the trio's victims.

Warning: This article contains descriptions of child abuse

Two of their victims, William and Meaghann Murphy, who are now 25 and 28, told BBC Scotland News the violence and cruelty they experienced as children became their normal reality.

News.title: Dutch broadcaster Avrotros pulls out of  2027 Eurovision Song Contest
News.content:
Dutch public broadcaster Avrotros has pulled out of next year's Eurovision Song Contest, saying that the competition can no longer be considered neutral while a participating country remains involved in a large-scale military conflict.

In a statement, external released on Monday, the broadcaster said the decision was due to a lack of clarity from organisers - the Eurovision Broadcasting Union (EBU) - over assessing which countries could compete.

Avrotros added: "The severe humanitarian suffering in Gaza and the ongoing restrictions on press freedom have contributed to increasing divisions surrounding the Eurovision Song Contest in recent years."

Earlier this month, the EBU updated their rules to state that if a country involved in an armed conflict wins the competition, it will be ineligible to host it the following year. But Avrotros said those changes "do not provide sufficient confidence that âthe â independent and neutral character of the Eurovision Song Contest has been restored."

The broadcaster's withdrawal from this year's contest in Burgas, Bulgaria, does not necessarily rule out Dutch participation in Eurovision 2027.

Another broadcaster within the Dutch public broadcasting system could potentially take it on as the country has several public broadcasters, unlike the UK.

But the Netherlands boycotted this year's contest in Vienna, Austria, after Israel were allowed to compete.

Only Ireland and Sweden have won Eurovision more than the Netherlands.

Martin Green, director of the contest, said in a statement that the EBU regretted Avrotros's decision but respected its views.

"We will now continue our dialogue with NPO, the umbrella organization for Dutch public service media, regarding the opportunities for another broadcaster to participate. We very much hope that audiences and artists in the Netherlands can continue to be represented in the Eurovision Song Contest."

News.title: 'Half my business will be gone' - firms in Canada and US fear trade war
News.content:
While the tariffs could mean changes for the Paloma Clothing company, other American companies are facing the same battle they have faced since Trump returned to office and began imposing his levies.

Bill Easton, owner of Terre Rouge Wines in Plymouth, California, has been unable to ship his wine north to Canada for the past year and a half due to a boycott of US alcohol.

He is currently paying $2,400 a month to store that wine in a warehouse in the hope that he will one day be able to ship it to the Canadian markets he sells to.

"The wine has just gotten better in the warehouse, but I can't expect my customer in Canada to pay that extra cost that I've assumed over the last year and a half as part of the price, if I was able to sell it tomorrow," Easton told the BBC.

And then there are the American businesses impacted by proximity to the Canadian border.

The number of Canadian customers travelling across the border to shop at Heather Seevers' craft shop, Northwest Yarns and Mercantile in Bellingham, Washington, has gone down some 20% since the tariff war began over a year ago. What has further irked Canadians has been Trump musing on Canada becoming a 51st US state.

The shop sits 25 minutes from the US-Canada border and since the "war" ensued Seevers said her business received emails from Canadian customers saying they could not patronise her business "due to anti-Canadian rhetoric".

"We completely understood that," she said.

But the combined impact of fewer customers and higher prices has left the shop asking for help from the community recently via a fundraising initiative to stay afloat.

And then, over the weekend, when the new tariffs struck, Seevers saw another hurdle appear.

"It's going to get worse before it gets better," she said. "It's going to take years and years and years to get a relationship back with Canada, and I think these new tariffs are digging us deeper into a hole."

Additional reporting from Nadine Yousif

News.title: 'It took 30 years to talk about my teacher raping me'
News.content:
It wasn't until 2022 when she had grief counselling that she confronted what had happened.

The following year she made a formal complaint to police.

"I am a mum now and my children are the age that I was then - and that cannot happen to them," she said.

She said finding the courage to contact police was difficult and it "took me a few days just to pluck up the courage".

Det Con Andrew Jones, from West Midlands Police's Major Crime Team, said: "I would like to express my gratitude to the brave woman who came forward to report what Allen had done to her as a child.

"She has been so brave throughout the investigation and court process."

Allen was sentenced at Birmingham Crown Court in July.

His defence argued the offence was committed during a difficult period in his life while he was experiencing anxiety.

But, during his sentencing remarks, His Honour Judge Paul Farrer KC, said he did not accept Allen's judgement was impaired at the time and said he had abused a position of trust.

That his offending remained undiscovered for more than three decades meant he was able to enjoy life in the community, the court heard.

It was noted the defendant was now in poor health, had diabetes, glaucoma and impaired hearing, had previously had a heart attack and might be experiencing the onset of Parkinson's disease.

The woman said it was not the sentencing but the guilty verdict that had been most important to her.

"I felt heard, I felt people have listened and they believe me," she added. "It is really validating and it raises your self-esteem a little bit, it means a lot."

News.title: Rain to return this week with chance of thunderstorms and flooding
News.content:
The weather is set to turn more unsettled this week as rain returns with a chance of thunderstorms and localised flooding.

Some places could see a return to showery conditions by Tuesday, but it is from Wednesday onwards that more widespread and persistent rain will arrive from the south.

The wet weather will be welcome for parched regions of the UK, but a lot more will be needed before drought conditions start to ease.

As well as the rain, temperatures will also be on the rise once more, as warmer air moving in could push midweek highs close to 27C (81F) in places.

News.title: Woman pleads guilty to breaching anonymity order in Jeffrey Donaldson case
News.content:
A 55-year-old Ballynahinch woman has pleaded guilty to breaching a lifetime anonymity order by posting information likely to reveal the alleged identity of a victim in the Jeffrey Donaldson sex abuse case.

Donna Toman of Lord Moira Park appeared at Downpatrick Magistrates' Court on Monday.

A defence lawyer said she was entering a guilty plea to a charge relating to a social media post earlier this year.

The charge states the post "was likely to lead members of the public to identify a person as the person against whom a qualifying offence is alleged to have been committed".

On 29 July police stated that the woman's arrest related to the Jeffrey Donaldson trial.

District Judge Magill said he wanted a pre-sentence report by 12 October adding that it was a "serious offence".

The court heard the offence can bring a six-month sentence.

Donaldson, who was an MP from 1997 until 2024, was convicted in June of 18 counts of sex abuse including one count of rape, which he committed against two women when they were children.

He was told by the judge that the sentence would be a lengthy one.

It has since been confirmed he is to appeal his convictions.

News.title: Pubs and hotels could see business rates reformed after review
News.content:
A review is being launched into the way business rates are calculated for pubs and hotels in England and Wales, and could lead to a reform of the system.

The Treasury says business rates expert Jerry Schurder will lead the review into rate valuations and report back in March 2027, with the government calling for the views of landlords, hoteliers and business owners to feed in to the process.

Last month, Andy Burnham announced a 20% cut in business rates for pubs, social clubs and live music venues in England, to come into effect in April.

Pub groups have argued they face disproportionately higher rates bills, but other businesses have called for a wider reform of the rates system.

According to the British Beer and Pub Association (BBPA), 161 pubs closed in the first three months of this year across England, Scotland and Wales, equating to the loss of around 2,400 jobs.

Rising business rates are cited as one issue facing the sector, although there have also been complaints that increases in National Insurance and the minimum wage have made staff costs more expensive.

James Murray, financial secretary to the Treasury, said the new review would look at "a rethink of valuations - so that we can build a fairer system for the future".

Emma McClarkin, chief executive of the BBPA, said: "For years pubs have paid a disproportionately higher business rates bill which has ground down their ability to keep the doors open, so this review is sorely needed and hugely welcome."

The BBPA says pubs are valued differently for rates than retail venues. Instead of being based just on floor area, they are judged by a measure called Fair Maintainable Trade (FMT) - which means when a pub's turnover increases, so does its rates bill.

Jonathan Lawson, the chief executive of Butcombe Group, which has 120 pubs across the south and south west of England, told the BBC's Today programme that the use of FMT meant pubs were effectively being "punished for success", while large online retailers that operate out of warehouses were not subject to revenue-based rates calculations.

Their rates, he said, "are calculated based on what is deemed to be the market rent for that area, and takes very little on board in terms of revenue driven through that site".

"You can have a very large site paying a relatively low level of business rates versus a relatively small pub... paying a very high level of business rates."

Schurder is a former business rates policy lead at advisory firm Newmark UK, and his review will feed into the next rates revaluation in 2029.

Northern Ireland and Scotland set their own valuations, while Wales presently chooses to align its methodology with England. As the same approach is used across England and Wales, the review will be looking for responses from both nations.

Schurder's appointment was welcomed by Craig Beaumont of the Federation of Small Businesses (FSB) who said he would bring "crucial heavyweight business rates expertise into the Treasury".

However, Beaumont said the government needed to address the wider business rates system and exempt more smaller firms by increasing the rates relief threshold for small businesses.

Jonny Haseldine from the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC) also said the review of valuations should be wider.

"The full reform of business rates, promised by the government at the last election, is urgently needed. This continued piecemeal approach to reform is the wrong approach," he said.

While the BCC said hospitality was the sector most worried about rates, Haseldine warned firms in every sector were struggling with the "complex and outdated" system.

Shadow Chancellor Sir Mel Stride said the review was "far too late for a sector this Labour government has already done its best to kill off".

"Tax hikes on business premises and jobs, alongside job-destroying regulation in the Employment Rights Act, have left many hospitality businesses on the brink," he said.

Liberal Democrat Treasury spokesperson Daisy Cooper said reform of business rates was "long overdue", but also called for an emergency VAT cut and a reverse to jobs tax changes "which have hammered hospitality in particular".

News.title: Girl gets tumour diagnosis 12 hours after eye test
News.content:
A mum said she "fell apart" after finding out her four-year-old daughter had a brain tumour, just 12 hours after an eye test.

Katie, 41, said her daughter Phoebe, now five, started to be sick and was getting severe headaches in February, but was told "it was just migraines" by a GP.

Following an eye test in May, Katie was called by the optician who told her to take her daughter straight to A&E at Addenbrooke's Hospital in Cambridge. Just hours later, she was diagnosed with a brain tumour.

"I fell apart and just sobbed and sobbed," said the mum from St Neots, Cambridgeshire. Thankfully, Phoebe's tumour was not cancerous and she is now under the care of specialists.

Katie said: "I felt like we were probably wasting the hospital's time because Phoebe was running around playing like normal but, looking back, she was probably the sickest kid there.

"I kept thinking, how am I going to tell her dad and the other children?

"I kept asking if Phoebe would survive but the doctors said they were unable to answer that at that time, which is the worst thing in the world as a parent."

News.title: Reform says it will prioritise British-born workers for social housing
News.content:
Tice said he wanted the rules on who was allocated a home to be changed away from need to suitability, putting British families, workers and veterans at the front of the queue, saying: "This comes down to fairness."

"We're saying that the first people we should be looking after are young, British workers - under 35, young British married couples, young British veterans - who have done the right thing," he said.

"They've got a job, they're doing their best, working in their community, setting a fine example, because the role of the British government is actually to look after British citizens first."

Rules would be changed to reserve at least half of all social homes in England for British-born workers aged under 35, with prioritisation also given to married couples, veterans, victims of domestic violence and care leavers.

Tice claimed there were currently 540,000 existing affordable social homes occupied by overseas nationals and he wanted that to change.

"It's not fair that young British working families can't get on the housing ladder when overseas nationals have come to the UK and, because of the current rules based on need rather than suitability, they have jumped ahead in the queue," he said.

"We just don't think that's right: I can't think of another country where you rock up with a family and you expect the local taxpayer in that country to pay for your housing needs."

UK or Irish nationals made up 88.5% of main social home householders in 2024/25, according to the English Housing Survey.

That means around 11.5% of main householders, the perÂ­son in whose name the social home is renÂ­ted, were non-UK or Irish nationÂ­als.

For its part, Reform estimates 540,000 social homes are currently occupied by foreign nationals.

Reform has previously announced it would evict foreign nationals from social housing - a plan criticised by housing charity Shelter which said building more homes is the solution, rather than "changing the order of the queue" and "stoking division".

Tice also said Reform would raise Â£10bn a year to build new homes, in part by reintroducing the Right to Buy scheme of the 1980s, allowing people to buy council homes at a discount.

"The failure then was they didn't reinvest the proceeds into building more affordable homes," he said, adding he believed reinvestment would raise a third of the investment needed to build 50,000 homes a year over a decade.

Tice said another third would be raised via housing authorities, and the final third would be money from local government pension schemes.

A Labour Party spokesperson said the plan was "unworkable and unserious", adding: "It would blow a Â£10bn blackhole in the public finances, would create years of wrangling with the EU, and could leave British citizens without a place to call home.

"This Labour government is investing billions to deliver the biggest boost to social and affordable housing in a generation, to fix the housing crisis we inherited from the Tories."

The Conservative Party, which also said it would revoke the right of foreign nationals to social housing, accused Reform of "trying to catch up" with its policies.

The Tories have said their plan, which would allow Irish citizens and some EU nationals to remain in social housing, would free up around 230,000 homes.

Sir James Cleverly, shadow housing secretary, added: "The Conservatives have already set out comprehensive plans to ensure British nationals are at the front of the queue for social housing. Now Reform are trying to catch up.

"We also believe in a home owning society and that those who work hard should be able to buy their own home, without unnecessary barriers standing in their way."

Liberal Democrat spokesperson Gideon Amos said that Reform's plan was a "cruel gimmick".

Green MP SiÃ¢n Berry said her party would tackle housing issues by ending Right to Buy, building and buying hundreds of thousands of new council homes, and introducing rent controls.

She added: "Another blatantly racist and cruel policy from Reform, adding to a host of plans to create a two-tier Britain â one for those born in the UK and one for everyone else."

News.title: CrossCountry to run full train service after power outage causes major disruption
News.content:
Train operator CrossCountry says it expects to run a full service on Monday after cancelling nearly all of its UK services the day before following a power cut at its control centre.

The outage in Birmingham at the weekend brought disruption from Glasgow to Penzance.

Major routes were affected between Birmingham and Manchester, which pass through Stoke-on-Trent, Coventry and Wolverhampton. Journeys from Leeds to York and Cheltenham to Cardiff were also caught in the travel chaos, leaving passengers frustrated.

On Monday morning, CrossCountry reported a handful of service cancellations, although these were put down to trains departing late and staff shortages.

Customers are advised to check their journey before travelling.

The operator on Sunday thanked passengers for their patience and understanding during the disruption.

Tickets purchased for travel on CrossCountry services on Sunday will be valid for travel on CrossCountry services until Wednesday, the company has said.

News.title: Wicker Man director's sons complete their late father's film trilogy
News.content:
Robin Hardy always envisaged his iconic 1973 folk horror film The Wicker Man as the first part of a trilogy.

The Wicker Tree, released in 2011, brought him closer to that ambition, but his death in 2016 at the age of 86 left the project incomplete.

Now his sons, Justin and Dominic, have been able to complete their father's trilogy, after finding a script for the final film.

Wrath of the Gods has its premiere at the FrightFest horror festival in London, external on Friday, a family dream made possible thanks to the surprise discovery of some long-lost family archive.

"The person who bought Justin's old family home said they'd discovered six sacks of letters, scripts and other material pertaining to Robin Hardy and The Wicker Man in the attic," says Dominic, an art historian at the University of Quebec in Montreal.

"Justin's first instinct was to burn them, but we couldn't ignore this original source material. Although we left it unopened for six months or more."

Number 10 has described the glorification of dangerous driving on social media as “utterly disgraceful” as the government ordered TikTok to take down videos “celebrating” a trend to drive in the wrong direction.

The intervention comes after two police officers – Pc Matthew Blades, 37, and Pc Tom Clough, 38 – died when the vehicle they were driving was struck head-on by a Volkswagen Passat travelling on the wrong side of the A66 in Teesside on Saturday night.

Five young men travelling in the Passat – Cole Robert Worthy, 17, Theo Rae, 17, Makai Saddington, 18, and 23-year-olds Michael Robert Cahill and Jacob Matusiak – were pronounced dead at the scene. One of the teenagers killed was involved in filming dangerous driving for TikTok before the fatal incident took place.

Andy Burnham criticised people who have posted videos of themselves driving recklessly on social media, telling reporters during a visit to Kyiv on Monday: “Anybody who glorifies dangerous driving is doing something that’s truly reprehensible.”

On Monday, No 10 condemned the practice, hitting out at those posting such videos “for clips and entertainment”. It is understood the government has contacted TikTok, which is already under investigation by Ofcom as part of a probe into whether the platform’s age checks are effective in preventing children from seeing harmful content.

A Downing Street spokeswoman said: “The glorification of dangerous driving for clips and entertainment is utterly disgraceful and that is why we have raised the issue of this appalling content with social media companies since the tragedy, and the Secretary of State for Culture, Media and Sport (Lisa Nandy) is clear that it should be removed in line with their legal obligations.”

open image in gallery Police officers at the scene of the fatal crash involving a police car and a Volkswagen Passat on the A66 ( PA )

Earlier on Monday, defence minister Luke Pollard said social media platforms should act to remove posts showing people driving the wrong way down roads, saying they would need to “step up”.

“There’s lots of content online on social media platforms of people celebrating dangerous driving, celebrating driving inappropriately on our roads down the wrong side of the roads, behaving incredibly badly,” he told BBC Breakfast.

“Now that’s a decision that social media companies have now. They’ve argued for many years they don’t need to be regulated, that they can police themselves. So this is a challenge for them. Remove that content.

“They know exactly what content is on their site. They know how their algorithm works. They also know that people post content to get views.

open image in gallery It is understood the government has contacted TikTok ( AFP/Getty )

“The more views you can get, sometimes you get money for it. So it’s a financial incentive for people to post outrageous content that gets more people watching it.”

He also told BBC Radio 5 Live that the government will be using powers in the Online Safety Act to compel platforms to take dangerous driving content down.

“But if the social media platforms were to regulate themselves and remove it in the first place, not allow their algorithm to share this type of content, because they know exactly what type of content that algorithm is designed to share, then I think we’d be in a better place,” he said.

The online safety regulator has said social media platforms are required under the Online Safety Act to minimise children’s exposure to content that encourages dangerous stunts and challenges.

An Ofcom spokesperson said: “Under the Online Safety Act, platforms must minimise children’s exposure to violent material and content promoting dangerous challenges.

“In July, we launched an investigation into TikTok’s compliance with its child safety duties, and we’ve shown we’ll take action if evidence suggests companies are falling short.”

open image in gallery PC Tom Clough (left) and PC Matthew Blades ( Cleveland Police )

TikTok has said its policies strictly prohibit content that could cause significant physical harm, including dangerous driving, and that it actively removes any videos and accounts that break its rules.

Meanwhile, court records show that Saddington was accused of assaulting a police officer and of causing racially aggravated alarm or distress to another in Middlesbrough on 9 June.

He had appeared before Teesside Magistrates’ Court on 17 July charged with the offences and was awaiting trial.

Cleveland Police had launched a pursuit after spotting the VW acting “suspiciously”, the force said in the aftermath of the fatal crash.

Officers began following the car in South Bank, near Middlesbrough in Teesside, before it joined the A66 in the wrong direction.

Officers ended their pursuit, but just 10 seconds later the VW collided with an oncoming police armed response unit at 3.39am. The police car, which was travelling in the right direction, was not part of the pursuit.

In tributes released by Cleveland Police, the two officers’ families said they had died “in the line of duty” and that their lives will “never be the same”.

open image in gallery Five young men travelling in the Passat – Cole Robert Worthy, 17, Theo Rae, 17, Makai Saddington, 18, and 23-year-olds Michael Robert Cahill and Jacob Matusiak – were pronounced dead at the scene. ( Facebook )

“He was our hero with a fantastic sense of humour,” PC Clough’s family said. “Jumped into action whenever needed, and willing to help anyone for any reason. Proudly fought for his country to make the world a better place. Always on public duty throughout his short life.”

In a separate tribute, PC Blades’ wife said he was a “devoted” father and her “best friend”.

Donations to a fundraiser set up by Cleveland Police to support the families of the two police officers have now reached more than £250,000. Organisers said funds raised would be split equally between the two officers’ families and the federation would continue to provide support.

A pregnant saleswoman was the victim of discrimination when her colleague told her "nobody wants to see a pregnant woman", a tribunal ruled.

Jessica Morgan, who was expecting, suggested she could give a presentation to a client when she was on the receiving end of the cruel comment from her co-worker.

Ms Morgan was told 'nobody wants to see a pregnant woman' give a presentation and was pressured into her giving her company car back early.

She previously had a 'close working relationship' with her colleague at a small sales firm that sold wood products.

However when she announced that she was pregnant, she noticed a 'shift' in his behaviour and he made the rude remark.

She said that she was not allowed to visit customers and to 'focus on being a mum'.

She also claimed that her boss said he 'wouldn't make the mistake of hiring a woman again' when discussing taking temporary cover.

After she left the role, an employment tribunal has now ruled that she had been the victim of pregnancy discrimination.

But, she didn't win her case because she brought the claim too late.

However she is still in line for compensation as she was found to have been victimised by her former employer.

Ms Morgan began working as a sales manager at Panelex Wood Agency, a wood supplier based in Swansea in April 2020.

She originally earned £40,000 a year at the small business where she worked alongside Frederick Geraint Hawkes who was in charge of procurement.

The pair had a 'close working relationship' and were in regular contact.

In July 2023 she told Mr Hawkes that she was pregnant and she claimed that there was a 'shift in his demeanour' at his point and she had a sense that he thought her pregnancy was an 'inconvenience'.

However it was found that the 'shift' was her anxiety increasing about being on maternity leave and her concerns about her position.

In November 2023, prior to going on maternity leave, Ms Morgan offered to assist Mr Hawkes in preparing for a presentation for a client.

He responded: "Nobody wants to see a pregnant woman Jess."

She claims that when discussing hiring temporary cover he said he 'wouldn't be making the mistake of hiring a woman again'.

Mr Hawkes denied making the comment.

open image in gallery Pregnant woman holding bump ( Getty/iStock )

Ms Morgan messaged a friend saying: "I’d walk out and start today if it was affordable ! Had some REALLT [sic] sexist comments thrown at me recently and making out I can’t do my job!

"Not allowed to visit customers anymore 'no one wants to see a pregnant woman' was what he said to me last week... I was upset!!”

However she felt unable to challenge the comments at the time.

Around the same time Mr Hawkes made comments about Ms Morgan being forgetful - yet the tribunal found that this was not connected to her pregnancy.

Ms Morgan began her maternity leave in January 2024 and she became anxious about her position - making jokes about 'having her back'.

However Mr Hawkes told her to 'focus on being a mum'.

In October 2024 they met up for a meeting in Costa to discuss her return to work where she was informed that her position no longer existed and they 'did not know where to put her'.

During the meeting Mr Hawkes said to her 'surely he [her partner] earns enough for you to stay at home'.

She left the meeting with the understanding that her employment would be brought to an end but she could keep her company car until Christmas and would be paid any outstanding money.

However Mr Hawkes later asked for the car back at the end of October.

Ms Morgan brought claims of unfair dismissal, wrongful dismissal, pregnancy discrimination, sex discrimination and victimisation to an employment tribunal in Swansea.

The victimisation claim was successful as was the pregnancy discrimination, however the latter was dismissed as it was brought out of time.

The other claims were all dismissed.

A hearing to determine her compensation will be made at a later date.

Employment Judge Alys Williams said: " In many ways therefore this is a sad case and it is unfortunate that the relationship has broken down to such a degree.

"We find that her failure to challenge the comments does not undermine her account.

"She refers in numerous messages to her partner that we have been taken to, to the futility of arguing with Mr Hawkes, something she expressed again in her oral evidence.

"She also only refers to ‘fighting back’ on one occasion, later in November 2023.

"We find [Ms Morgan] did not frequently challenge Mr Hawkes and in light of the nature of their relationship, the dependency, anxiety and desire to please we describe above we are satisfied that her failure to challenge does not undermine her account.

"We are satisfied the comment does amount to unfavourable treatment. It suggests that the way a pregnant woman looks will make her off-putting to clients to the extent that she should not be seen.

"We find that the request for [Ms Morgan] to return the company car amounts to a detriment.

"[Ms Morgan] agreed to the termination of her employment on terms, including that she could keep the company car untilChristmas.

"[Panelex] reneged on that agreement very soon thereafter and as soon as [Ms Morgan] sought payment of the sums to which she was entitled.

"The request to return the company car was as a direct response (couched in terms of a ‘compromise’) to [Ms Morgan's] request for the wages legally owed to her.

"The car was used as a bargaining chip for [Ms Morgan] to receive that money which she had made clear from the outset she desperately needed."

A suspected arson attack took place at an industrial estate used for parking by holidaymakers flying from Gatwick Airport, raising fears several customers may have been impacted.

The blaze happened at Caldryne Business Park in Rowfant, five miles from the airport, on Saturday night.

Dramatic pictures showed flames dominating the skyline as teams of firefighters worked to tackle the incident while police shut off the immediate area. The next day, images emerged showing the blackened remains of dozens of vehicles at the industrial estate.

After the incident, Sussex Police arrested a 67-year-old man on suspicion of arson. On Monday morning, the force said he had been bailed as investigations continued.

Were you impacted? Email alexander.ross@independent.co.uk

open image in gallery A 67-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of arson in connection with the fire(Joe Giddens/PA) ( PA Archive )

Meanwhile, both the police and West Sussex Fire and Rescue Service have issued alerts to people who have may left their vehicle at the industrial estate for holiday parking.

A force spokesperson said: “A number of cars were damaged at a site used for holiday parking. Any affected consumers are advised to contact their operator directly.”

The fire service said the blaze, which it described as “significant and complex”, involved a workshop, vehicles and cylinders. It also led the loss of electricity for surrounding homes.

On Monday, a service spokesperson said: “Fire crews have been at the scene this morning damping down hotspots, and we are hoping to leave the scene later on today. Fortunately there were no casualties as a result of this fire.

"A joint fire investigation is now ongoing with Sussex Police.”

Following the fire, a number of fundraisers were launched for businesses impacted by the fire. On GoFundMe, Ashley Riley, from The Bears Banger Racing Team, said his team and family had “lost everything in the fire.”

The fundraiser to help “get life back on track and to rebuild their business from scratch”, had reached £6,237.

So, it’s almost time to plant your spring bulbs – or is it?

With the ground still rock hard following a sweltering summer, gardeners are advised to at least delay planting bulbs until rain has softened the earth.

“It’s better to wait for the soil to cool a bit more before planting but on the flip side, it’s still good to get into garden centres and choose the varieties you want early while there’s the best selection,” says Ian Clark, Taylors Bulbs marketing manager. “But it’s definitely better to wait for some rain to make planting easier.”

“Bulbs are at their most dormant at the moment and the most important time for them is late spring/early summer after flowering when they are taking in moisture and nutrients for the following year,” he continues.

open image in gallery ‘On the flip side, it’s still good to get into garden centres and choose the varieties you want early while there’s the best selection,’ says Ian Clark ( Alamy/PA )

“Hot weather earlier in the summer had a small effect on tulip growth but not too serious, more likely that the bulbs haven’t got quite as big as they might have done had they had more favourable growing conditions.”

“Even if you put them in the ground now, they would stay dormant until we get rain anyway, because moisture initiates root growth,” says Ashley Edwards, head gardener at Crocus.

When it comes to planting, place your bulbs deeper than you normally would. This will expose them to more moisture.

Can you still plant bulbs in pots in early autumn?

“Pots are different because you’re going to be watering your pots anyway. You could even start bulbs off in pots and then transfer them into the ground when the rain does come,” says Edwards.

open image in gallery Good candidates for pots include narcissi, crocuses and imperial fritillaries ( Alamy/PA )

Good candidates for pots include narcissi, crocuses and imperial fritillaries, he recommends, along with hyacinths for scent.

Leave tulips until later

Tulips do have a preference to be planted in cooler soil later in the autumn, and it is better to wait if you can, Adam Taylor, director of Taylors Bulbs, advises.

Tulips, in particular, benefit from being planted in November or even December, when there’s less danger they will succumb to tulip fire, a fungal disease similar to grey mould.

Will those left in the ground survive?

“If spring-flowering bulbs have been left in gardens from last year, I would expect very few detrimental effects particularly with the early flowering types such as crocus, hyacinth and narcissus,” says Taylor.

“They have been dormant throughout this summer and if we have some moisture for them to start rooting when the soil temperature drops, I expect them to come again next spring without significant issue.

open image in gallery ‘If spring-flowering bulbs have been left in gardens from last year, I would expect very few detrimental effects particularly with the early flowering types such as crocus,’ says Taylor ( PA )

“However, in those areas where we experienced the dry weather in late May, it’s possible that any later spring flowering bulbs left in the ground such as narcissus and particularly the type of tulips that can flower perennially (Darwin hybrid, fosteriana and species types), the leaves will have died back quicker than they may normally do.

“This will mean the plant was under stress at a time when it will have been creating the new bulbs for next year and/or making the flower bud for next spring’s flower.

“It’s slightly possible in some areas and some circumstances that there may be fewer flowers than hoped but nature will recover this for the year after, should we receive more normal conditions next spring.

“In the meantime, planting some fresh bulbs in those areas will only help fill any gaps that may come in next year’s display.”

Edwards adds: “If they are very congested there’s a chance they could dry out and they might come up blind (without flowers) next year.”

As for tulips, some are more resilient than others when they’ve been left in the ground, such as Tulipa ‘Ballerina’ and ‘Queen of Night’, while many parrot tulips are less reliable, Edwards observes.

open image in gallery As for tulips, some are more resilient than others when they’ve been left in the ground, such as Tulipa ‘Ballerina’ and ‘Queen of Night’ ( PA )

“I think we should be going more towards the species tulips now because they are adapted to heat, they come from Iran, Turkey and those areas of the world and are used to growing in quite mountainous areas. A lot of them are very resilient and they spread as well.”

What about bulbs you’ve stored?

“The hot weather will accentuate any underlying issues in bulbs such as fusarium in tulips and base rot in daffodils, meaning you see it sooner,” says Clark.

If you lifted this year’s spring-flowering bulbs after flowering, you need to have stored them somewhere cool to reduce the likelihood of deterioration. If your once-cool garden shed has become a hothouse, it may affect your bulbs, says Edwards.

open image in gallery ‘The hot weather will accentuate any underlying issues in bulbs such as fusarium in tulips and base rot in daffodils, meaning you see it sooner,’ says Clark ( Alamy/PA )

“Sometimes the garage is better because it is better insulated than sheds,” he points out. “Sheds can obviously get really hot and if the bulbs are shrivelled or you press them and they crumble under your fingers, then they are too dry and not worth planting.”

Bulbs such as alliums, crocuses and daffodils are a bit tougher, he notes.

“Just test them, make sure there’s no mould on them and they haven’t got any powdery fungal diseases. You need to test the firmness of the bulb.”

News.title: Major UK-funded climate project in Bangladesh forced to close over aid cuts
News.content:
