World.title: Translation Cutbacks Limit International Access to North Macedonia’s Literature
World.content:
For a small country of just under two million people, with a small language and an even smaller literary market, getting books translated and published abroad can be crucial to keeping its literature visible beyond its borders.

But for the past two years, Macedonian authors and publishers have had one fewer tool to help them do that. A government programme that provided grants to foreign publishers willing to translate and publish Macedonian books has been suspended since 2024.

The good news is that the Culture Ministry told BIRN there is a “real possibility” it will relaunch a redesigned translation programme later this year. But the bad news is how many excellent books have been denied a wider readership over the last two years.

The Ministry says it typically allocated between one to four million denars [16,000- 65,000 euros] a year for the programme. In 2024, around 84,000 euros was distributed through 31 contracts with foreign publishers. Foreign publishers interested in Macedonian literature could apply to North Macedonia’s Culture Ministry for funding to cover translation costs, reducing the financial risk of publishing authors who are largely unknown in their markets.

Without that incentive, publishers say, some potentially valuable translations simply do not happen. “Our success at international book fairs, such as Frankfurt, is diminished,” says Bojan Sazdov, editor-in-chief of the publishing house TRI and president of the Macedonian Association of Publishers.

“When there is interest in translating a Macedonian book, we can no longer point publishers to the programme as a way of obtaining funding for the translation.”

World.title: Hanging Out: Serbia’s Ruling Party Funfair is About Suppressing Voter Turnout
World.content:
Without Novi Sad’s EXIT Festival, this year’s summer entertainment in Serbia was provided by the ruling Progressive Party funfair.

After a long day visiting factories, inspecting schools, roadworks and parks, government ministers, advisers, and local authorities hung out with people under white tents.

The show included music, dancing, feasting, and live television broadcasts.

Just in the first 18 days of August, President Aleksandar Vucic made 64 live appearances on Serbian TV, according to the Centre for Research, Transparency and Accountability, CRTA.

Not quite a formal election campaign, if you ask Vucic. Something between a ‘presidential tour’ and a prequel to the actual election campaign that everyone expects in the autumn.

Such media domination is familiar to those who follow populism; party leaders skip formal institutions and speak directly to the people.

When this media takeover combines with the atmosphere of a village fair, people tend to ask private questions publicly. Here’s where the media literacy classes provided by Serbia’s tabloids begin paying off.

World.title: Seven Days: Ukrainian Recalls Captivity at Hands of Bosnian Serb
World.content:
Mykola said he spent most of his captivity in a forest pit between the villages of Shybene and Krasny Rih. He said his hands were tied and there were rats in the pit. When he killed one after it bit him, he said a soldier hit him in the head with a rifle butt. The soldier told him: “Kill another one and I’ll shoot you.”

Mykola said he saw other captives being tortured.

According to the Ukrainian Media Initiative for Human Rights, MIHR, which inspected the site, the pits were some 90 centimetres deep; those inside had to sit in water; they lost feeling in their legs; and they had to urinate and defecate in the same spot.

Lidiia Tarash, a journalist and head of the documentation department of MIHR, said the researchers were led to the site by Mykola. A dead body was found in one of the pits, as well as the remains of Russian military rations, fortifications and ammunition boxes.

MIHR identified five locations in the area where civilians were held and documented the capture of 43 individuals. Its findings helped lead to the indictment of Savicic. Multiple interlocutors said Serbs were among the Russian forces. Everyone named Savicic as being in charge, Tarash said.

In late May last year, the X account of Milorad Dodik, then the president of Bosnia’s predominantly Serb-populated Republika Srpska entity, published a photo of himself visiting the representative office of the Serbian Orthodox Church in Russia. Savicic was in the photo.

Britain imposed sanctions on him in November 2024.

Mykola said Savicic and his unit are the reason he still has trouble sleeping at night. His back was damaged during his captivity and he said he is haunted by the word ‘liberation’, which he heard over and over again from his captors.

“They kept saying: ‘We came to liberate you.’ But liberate me from what? From a normal life?”

Savicic’s trial is a matter of justice and responsibility, he said.

“None of them can say: ‘I was just following orders’ and to think they aren’t responsible for it,” Mykola told BIRN. “Someone gave you an order, but it was still your choice whether to execute it.”

World.title: Saudi Dissident, Held by Bulgaria Since 2021, is Freed
World.content:
A photo of Abdulrahman al-Khalid that was distributed at a demonstration calling for his release in March in Sofia.

Saudi dissident and human rights activist Abdulrahman al-Khalidi was freed on Friday, having spent almost five years in administrative detention in Bulgaria after he was designated as a threat to public security.

“Abdulrahman has just been freed following a modification of the control measure,” activist and publisher Victor Lilov. who has long campaigned for al-Khalidi’s release, confirmed to BIRN.

The Bulgarian Helsinki Committee NGO, which also confirmed al-Khalidi’s release, described his four years and ten months of custody as “one of the most prolonged cases of detention of an asylum seeker in Bulgaria”.

Al-Khalidi has been kept in detention centres in Bulgaria since October 2021 and has reportedly been subjected to beatings by police, suffered from dire living conditions and a lack of transparency over the reasons for his detention.

For most of this time, he was held in the Butmantsi Detention Centre on the outskirts of the Bulgarian capital Sofia. In January 2026 he was transferred to a temporary accommodation centre for foreigners in Lyubimets, near the border with Turkey.

“After almost five years of detention, this is an extremely important moment … Thank you for standing with me throughout all these years,” al-Khalidi wrote to supporters on Facebook as he was being transferred from Lyubimets to Sofia’s Migration Directorate.

Al-Khalidi’s lawyer, Diana Radoslavova from the Voice in Bulgaria Centre for Legal Aid, explained to BIRN that his release happened because he was about to compete the maximum term for which people can be held in migration detention, 18 months. He had previously been held in asylum detention.

Radoslavova was with al-Khalidi after he was released. She said the first thing he did was speak with his wife and children.

“He’s doing extremely surprisingly well, for me. He’s psychologically a very strong person because this is not an easy transition for him,” she said.

Al-Khalidi became politically active in Saudi Arabia around the time of the Arab Spring protests. Interviewed by BIRN in 2024, he explained that political arrests, often followed by death sentences, were frequent in late 2012 to early 2013. That is why he decided to leave the country in 2013.

He continued his activism abroad, also working as a journalist writing articles critical of the Saudi government. According to Human Rights Watch, he was part of late Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi’s movement, called the Bees Army, which sought to counter pro-Saudi government propaganda.

After leaving Saudi Arabia, he lived in exile in Qatar, Egypt and Turkey, where his wife, son and daughter still live.

In 2021 his Saudi documents were about to expire. The only way to renew them would have been to enter the Saudi embassy in Istanbul, the same embassy where Khashoggi was killed in 2018. To avoid Saudi officials, he decided to apply for asylum at the Bulgarian border. That is when Bulgarian authorities first placed him in detention in response to information passed on by the State Agency for National Security that the applicant posed a national security threat.

In April 2024, despite the Supreme Administrative Court in Sofia’s decision that he was eligible to receive asylum, the State Refugee Agency and the State Agency for National Security continued to keep him detained on the grounds that he was a threat to public security.

His case has been taken to the European Court of Human Rights, where a verdict is still awaited. In March 2026, 18 MEPs wrote an official letter to the Bulgarian government expressing concerns regarding his detention conditions and calling on Bulgaria to comply with legal decisions.

In recent years, multiple instances of Bulgaria denying asylum or deporting people under questionable conditions have come to light, as well as cases of police brutality, such as recent allegations of widespread violence against migrants being held in a detention centre in Pastrogor.

World.title: Week in Review: Momentous Moves and Dubious Intentions
World.content:
Last week Turkey adopted a momentous law on the disarmament of the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK). Many see the law as a major step towards ending the decades-long conflict with the Kurdish militants. In return for disarmament, the law foresees supervised release and postponed sentencing for many of those convicted of being involved in the PKK.

While the end of the conflict with the PKK would be welcome news for Turkey, many still wonder what motives are driving the ruling party and President Recep Tayyip Erdogan to pursue such a deal. For many ordinary Kurds, there is still trepidation over whether they will truly see an improvement in their rights and freedoms.

World.title: EU Questions Serbia’s Turn to Russia for Help in Battling Wildfires
World.content:
After Russia sent an aircraft to assist with wildfire fighting in Serbia, the European Commission said late Thursday that it is also ready to provide assistance, but EU candidate state Serbia hasn’t yet activated the bloc’s Civil Protection mechanism.

“Should Serbia activate in the upcoming hours/days in response to wildfires, we will immediately coordinate with European partners to mobilise assistance in line with actual needs and the situation on the ground,” a European Commission spokesperson told BIRN.

There are 20 active wildfires in Serbia, Luka Causic, head of the Interior Ministry’s Department for Emergency Situations, said on Thursday. The situation is most dire in the Deliblato Sands nature reserve, which has been battling wildfires since late July.

Following a request from Serbia, the European Commission provided satellite imagery to support the response of local firefighters.

However, Serbia turned to Russia for air support. A Russian Emercom Il-76 aircraft arrived in Serbia on Wednesday evening, said Serbian Interior Minister Ivica Dacic.

“The aircraft can drop up to 42 tonnes of water in a single pass, making it one of the most powerful operational firefighting aircrafts, given that there are currently no firefighting aircraft of this capacity available within the EU Civil Protection Mechanism,” Dacic wrote on Instagram on Wednesday.

The Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs wrote on X on Wednesday evening that “the Serbian side appealed to Russia for assistance amid a critical wildfire situation and growing threats to populated areas”.

“Russia consistently supports the brotherly Serbian people,” it added.

However, the European Commission spokesperson declared that “relations with Russia and Putin’s regime cannot be ‘business as usual’”.

“When it comes to the support received from Russia, let us reiterate that the EU wants to count on Serbia as a reliable partner,” the spokesperson said.

On Sunday, Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic said that both the EU and Russia had offered to help with wildfires in Serbia, but that help was not needed at the moment.

“I would like to thank Ursula von der Leyen for the fact that she has included us on the map of countries at risk, and for ensuring that European mechanisms are monitoring the events here, meaning that we can expect assistance at any moment,” he said.

“The Russians have also offered us support and assistance, but it is not necessary at this point. We have sufficient forces, expertise and helicopters to deal with this situation ourselves,” Vucic added.

Serbia has been part of the EU Civil Protection Mechanism since 2015. Participating countries can request assistance via the mechanism when the scale of an emergency overwhelms the response capabilities of a country.

World.title: Thaci Expects Acquittal as Hague Court’s War Crimes Verdict Nears
World.content:
Hashim Thaci with co-defendant Rexhep Selimi (R) in court in The Hague, April 2023. Photo: EPA/Koen van Weel/Pool.

Former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci said in an interview broadcast on Thursday evening that he anticipated being acquitted of all charges in the war crimes and crimes against humanity case against him and three other former Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA leaders at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague.

The verdict in the case against Thaci, Kadri Veseli, Rexhep Selimi and Jakup Krasniqi is expected on September 16.

“I expect to be acquitted of every charge. I have nothing to add to the arguments of the defence team or to my final statement in the courtroom,” Thaci said in the written interview with the Pristina-based broadcaster RTV Dukagjini.

The four men are accused of individual and command responsibility for crimes committed against prisoners held at KLA detention facilities in Kosovo and in neighbouring Albania, including 102 murders. The crimes were allegedly committed during and just after the Kosovo War in 1998 and 1999.

All four defendants have pleaded not guilty.

Thaci said he did not regret supporting the creation of the Kosovo Specialist Chambers when he was in office, but said he had not expected the decision by Kosovo’s elected representatives to be “misused so brutally”.

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers was created specifically to try former members of the KLA. It is located in The Hague and staffed by international judges and prosecutors due to doubts about the Kosovo justice system’s ability to try former KLA fighters, many of whom are considered heroes in Kosovo.

In the interview, Thaci spoke about a 2010 report by former Swiss Council of Europe rapporteur Dick Marty, which alleged serious crimes including organ-trafficking by KLA-linked figures. The report ultimately led to the establishment of the Kosovo Specialist Chambers. Thaci claimed that its allegations were developed with the involvement of officials at the Council of Europe from Serbia and Russia – both of which oppose Kosovo’s independence.

“The freedom and the construction of Kosovo’s independence were unswallowable for Serbia and Russia. After failing to delegitimise it at the International Court of Justice [which ruled that Kosovo’s independence declaration did not violate international law], they turned to the Council of Europe. The aim was clear: to discredit the state of Kosovo,” he said.

Thaci also criticised the prosecution’s treatment of defence witnesses and evidence in his trial.

He accused prosecutors of giving greater weight to what he described as “fabricated testimony” originating from the time when Slobodan Milosevic was in power in Belgrade, and dismissing testimony from senior Western and international officials who were “the eyes and ears” in Kosovo.

“The prosecution is elevating evidence fabricated during the era of the Milosevic regime, and ignoring the testimony of senior officials from the US, NATO, Britain, the UN, the OSCE and other international institutions,” he said.

Thaci noted that the appearance of such international figures as defence witnesses demonstrated their concern about the proceedings.

“It is not easy for these personalities to sit in such a courtroom. I understood that they were seeing that something wrong was happening in this process. They felt a moral obligation to tell the truth,” he said.

Thaci declined to comment on the current Kosovo government’s approach to the Specialist Chambers.

Asked whether his rights had been violated during the proceedings, he replied that he considered the “process as a whole” to have involved violations.

He also criticised the decision not to release him on bail, saying that the arguments used against his release were based on “prejudices and hypotheses”. Thaci said several NATO member states had offered guarantees on his behalf and that he remained grateful to them.

During the trial, the prosecution attempted to prove that, as members of the KLA General Staff, they were responsible for lower-ranking fighters who committed crimes. The defence argued that the KLA did not have a proper army command structure, so the defendants did not have real authority over lower-ranking KLA fighters.

Thaci resigned as Kosovo’s president in November 2020 to face the charges and together with the other three men was sent to detention in The Hague, where they have been ever since. The trial started in April 2023.

During the trial, KLA veterans and their supporters have staged protests in Pristina, Tirana, Skopje, Strasbourg and The Hague, accusing the Specialist Chambers of bias.

In 2024, Thaci was also charged with obstruction of justice, alongside four others, including former Kosovo Justice Minister Hajredin Kuci. The trial for this case started in February, days after proceedings in the war crimes and crimes against humanity trial ended. Thaci and the four others accused of obstruction of justice – Kuci, Isni Kilaj, Bashkim Smakaj and Fadil Fazliu – have denied wrongdoing.

World.title: Zadar Was the Most Expensive Croatian City in July
World.content:
August the 24th, 2026 – Zadar was the most expensive Croatian city of all in July, with strong economic growth very much being a double edged sword for the area.

Buying basic groceries has long been a negotiation with one’s own wallet for people in Croatia, but in July, the toughest conditions spilled over onto the area of Zadar County. The basic consumer basket for a four-member family here reached a record 498 euros, reports HRT. Morski writes that a basic daily trip to the shop or the market has become a source of stress for many, and citizens openly complain about the constant quiet price rises:

a previously bustling market sits almost empty

“Vegetables have become very expensive, they get used up quickly, you need a lot of them. Fruit is also very expensive and it seems to me that meat has gone up, fish has also gone up a lot,” says Zadar resident Katja. For pensioners, the situation is even more alarming. Every single purchase requires calculation and a search for discounts: “I really don’t go to the shops much. You buy where you can according to your wallet and that’s it, and yes it’s expensive, it’s definitely expensive, this isn’t for us pensioners, it’s abnormal,” is the honest assessment of Zorica, who lives on the Zagreb–Zadar route.

That consumer habits are changing and that people are buying significantly less than in previous years was confirmed to us by the sellers themselves. Zadar’s market, which in July should be bustling with local and foreign visitors, at times looks unusually empty.

Seller Rada briefly summarises the problem: “Everything is expensive, the shops too.” Her colleague Ilonka points out that even regular customers have thinned out their visits: “There are no customers. I normally have my own customers, but look, two people are walking through the market.”

the price of rapid expansion

How did it come about that Zadar took the top spot for the most expensive groceries? Experts explain that the answer lies in a specific economic effect of the rapid expansion of the regional economy.

Assoc. Prof. Dr. Jurica Bosna, Head of the Department of Economics at the University of Zadar, clarifies the background to this trend: “Nobody wants to have the most expensive basket of goods, but it still shows that the county is developing strongly, and this is an effect known in economics, when we grow faster than we perhaps should according to some optimal economic rates, then it’s unfortunately inevitable that inflation will develop and that the result will be like this,” he stated.

While macroeconomic indicators record the growth and development of the whole of Zadar County, for the general public, that statistic brings no comfort whatsoever. The vicious circle in which the economy advances strongly while prices rise in an unbridled way leaves the deepest mark on household budgets. Since wages and pensions do not come close to keeping pace, the consumer baskets of Zadar residents remain ever emptier.

World.title: Meet the Croatian Road Often Compared to the Legendary Route 66
World.content:
August the 24th, 2026 – There’s an incredibly scenic Croatian road frequently compared to the legendary Route 66 across the pond in the USA – and a drive along it is nothing less than breathtaking.

When someone mentions Route 66, most people immediately think of the endless American highway, old motels, neon signs and kilometres of asphalt running through some of the most famous landscapes of the United States. Few realise that Croatia has its own very interesting road with the same number in Croatia as well. It goes without saying that Croatia’s D66 doesn’t have thousands of kilometres or hold the status of an American icon, but because of the designation it carries and the landscapes it passes through, it resembles the US legend in many ways.

Putni kofer writes that it has been referred to many times as the Istrian version of Route 66 and presented it as a road that evokes old, nostalgic Istria. Today, the impressive D66 connects Pula, Labin and Vozilići with Opatija, and according to the official decision on the classification of public roads it is about 90 kilometres long. Still, if the goal is to find its most spectacular part, one should head towards the eastern coast of Istria, that is, towards Plomin.

the most impressive section begins at plomin

Plomin is an excellent place to start this short road trip. The old fortified little town sits on a hill above Plomin Bay, and right by the D66 there is also a rest area with a viewpoint. A few kilometres further on there is another spot from which the view opens towards the Kvarner Bay, Cres and Lošinj.

After that begins the stretch that makes it worth driving this road slowly. The asphalt winds under the slopes of Učka, the sea is almost constantly somewhere in sight, and on the other side of the Kvarner Cres appears. In certain places the road runs high enough above the coast that the view feels almost like from a large natural balcony. The greatest advantage of state road D66 is precisely that, over a relatively short distance, viewpoints, medieval places, steep coastline and well-known Kvarner resorts alternate.

the stunning Brseč, a town from 1102 towering above at 157 metres above the sea

SONY DSC

One of the places worth turning off the road for is Brseč. D66 reaches it after driving along the slopes of Učka, and the old part of the settlement is situated on a cliff 157 metres high above the expanse of Kvarner. The first written records of Brseč date back to 1102, although the area was inhabited much earlier. It is particularly interesting that the history of Brseč is also directly linked to the road that passes this way. The Tourist Board of Mošćenička Draga notes that the economic development of the place in the 19th century was spurred by the new road from Pula towards Plomin, then Brseč and Mošćenice and further towards Rijeka.

Today the medieval character of Brseč can still be felt in the narrow streets and passages of the old town core. From the cliff by the little church of St Magdalene one of the most beautiful views in the area opens up, while from the western entrance to the place Cres can be seen. Beneath the high rocks a completely different world is hidden. Between Brseč and Mošćenička Draga lie the beaches of Uboka and Jelenšćica, which can be reached on foot via paths that descend from the main road. The coastline in this area is extremely indented, with steep cliffs, tiny coves and stone fishermen’s cottages by the sea.

from ancient towns to well-known resorts

After Brseč the scenery changes again. D66 continues towards Mošćenička Draga, one of the best-known places at the foot of Učka. The road approaches the sea, and the high rocks gradually give way to beaches and a more built-up coastline. Mošćenička Draga developed from a fishing harbour, and today it is especially known for the long pebble beach of Sipar. Its pebbles were formed by the action of the stream that descends from the slopes of Učka and the sea that has shaped them over the years.

Just a few kilometres further on lies Medveja, another place along the D66 with a long pebble beach. After it comes Lovran, where the whole drive takes on a more elegant appearance. Instead of the almost wild coast around Brseč, old villas, gardens and houses appear along the road that recall the time when this part of the Kvarner became one of the favourite resorts of Central Europe.

just over 90 kilometres from pula to opatija

The entire D66 from Pula to Opatija is a little over 90 kilometres long, but for a panoramic outing the stretch from Plomin to Opatija is especially interesting. According to the kilometres listed on the EuroVelo 8 route, from the Plomin area to Opatija it is roughly thirty kilometres of driving.

That may not sound like much, but that is precisely the charm of this road. In a short drive one passes Plomin Bay, open views towards Cres and Lošinj, medieval Brseč, the steep slopes of Učka, Mošćenička Draga, Medveja, Lovran and finally Opatija. Although it forms part of the Croatian cycling route EuroVelo 8, this road should not be imagined as a lonely carriageway without cars. On the official route website traffic on certain sections is marked as moderate, and from Medveja towards Rijeka as heavy, so if you decide to cover it on four wheels, extra caution is recommended for cyclists.

World.title: Drniš Bypass Construction to Benefit Šibenik Port
World.content:
August the 24th, 2026 – The future Drniš bypass will greatly benefit the local economy, as well as Šibenik Port directly.

The construction of the second and third phases of the complex Drniš bypass project has begun, with the client being Hrvatske ceste (Croatian roads), and the contractor being the consortium of Texo Molior from Cavtat and CGP Slovenia.

Transport Minister Butković pointed out that after securing the financial structure and signing the contract, work on the project is now starting. Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that he also noted that it is a technically complex intervention with a route that includes two overpasses, two viaducts and a bridge over the Čikola River. Speaking about the continuation of activities on the future Šibenik–Drniš–Knin expressway, Minister Butković highlighted that the preparation of project documentation for the section from Drniš towards the Oklaj interchange is in an advanced stage.

a 34 million euro investment

After the design of that phase is completed, a tender is planned to be issued, so the project is being gradually prepared for phased implementation. He also referred to the reconstruction of state roads DC56 and DC33, which connect the Drniš area with Split and Knin respectively, and whose total reconstruction value is around 34 million euros. After the design of that phase is completed, a tender is planned to be issued, gradually preparing the project for implementation.

“A tender has already been issued for one, the other is in preparation, so there will be a great deal of investment in road infrastructure here in the area of the town of Drniš and Šibenik-Knin County,” added Minister Butković. Šibenik-Knin County Prefect Paško Rakić stressed that the Drniš bypass is of great importance for the entire county, especially for the traffic connection of its hinterland, and that residents of the wider Drniš and Knin areas will use it.

“The Šibenik–Drniš–Knin expressway, as well as this bypass, is the backbone of Šibenik-Knin County in terms of traffic, and it is as important to us as the Pelješac Bridge,” emphasised Prefect Rakić. “This is historic for us,” emphasised Drniš Mayor Tomislav Dželalija, noting that generations of Drniš residents have waited decades for this project.

a massive development boost for the area

Expressing satisfaction that the works were ceremonially started today, he pointed out that the removal of transit traffic, along with increased traffic safety, will create additional preconditions for the expansion of the economic zone and the further development of the town. He added that the Government of the Republic of Croatia, through strong investments including road and railway infrastructure, is giving impetus to the town’s development, and thanked them for the projects being implemented in the Drniš area.

President of the Management Board of Hrvatske ceste Ivica Budimir emphasised that the project has a broader economic significance for Drniš, especially because of the direct connection of the industrial zone with the Šibenik port.

“After this road is constructed, the industrial zone in the entire Drniš area will develop significantly faster, better and to a higher quality, and become much more competitive,” emphasised Budimir. Speaking about the technical demands of the project, he added that almost ten percent of the route consists of viaducts, while the most significant structure is the large bridge over the Čikola River canyon, with a span of 220 metres, along with a series of other structures along the route.

World.title: Baćina Lakes – Meet Croatia’s Freshwater Phenomenon
World.content:
August the 24th, 2026 – Baćina Lakes are Croatia’s freshwater phenomenon, with water warmer than that in the sea and the ability to swim year-round.

If you’ve ever driven from Makarska down toward Dubrovnik, you’ll have passed by them. You probably glanced left for a second, spotted a blue patch amid the greenery, and continued on toward the sea. Yet there, just a few kilometres from Ploče, lies something no other Croatian town has: seven lakes within the boundaries of a single town. They are called the Baćina Lakes and bear names that sound like a list from an old book: Oćuša, Crniševo, Podgora, Sladinac, Šipak, Plitko Lake, and Vrbnik.

Putni kofer writes that six of them are interconnected by narrow passages, so you can paddle or boat from one into another, while Vrbnik, which is also the smallest, is completely separate from the rest. Together they cover about 138 hectares.

they’re warmer than the sea

The Baćina Lakes form a cryptodepression, meaning their surface is only slightly above sea level, while their bottoms lie deep below it. Although they are just a step from the sea and surrounded by permeable limestone, the lakes are freshwater. Some springs are nevertheless directly connected to the sea, so salt water appears in the deeper layers. In the Klokun area near Plitko Lake there is a spring that supplies drinking water to the town of Ploče and the surrounding area.

During the scorching summer, the water in the lakes is noticeably warmer than the sea, with tourist sources citing a difference of roughly three degrees. Because of this, the swimming season here starts earlier and ends later than on the coast. The best-known bathing spots are those near the Mindel spring, and the hidden coves and small beaches are reached by kayak, paddleboard, or traditional Neretva boat.

links with queen teuta

Legend has it that the Illyrian Queen Teuta adored this area, and the lakes are still called Teuta’s pearls. Historians, however, have their own evidence and explanations. Near Sladinac Lake the remains of the Roman settlement of Praetoria have been found, along with the remains of an early Christian basilica from the 6th century and a necropolis of stećci tombstones.

Around the lakes a walking and cycling path about 15 kilometres long has been arranged, with benches, springs, and information boards. In 2020 the Public Institution for Protected Natural Areas of Dubrovnik-Neretva County installed 19 educational boards about dragonflies, amphibians, reptiles, and birds. Near the Oćuša spring there is a bird-watching hide, and the lakes also contain three small islets, one of which is named the Island of Love. The entire area forms part of the Natura 2000 ecological network, within two zones of the Neretva Delta, as a habitat for strictly protected and endemic species.

a worthwhile stop off on a long drive south…

A visit to the Baćina Lakes is truly an experience you will remember for a lifetime. Walking the paths that wind right beside the lakes will reveal scenes covered in water lilies, the reflection of clouds mirrored on the still water, and the song of rare birds that creates an almost meditative atmosphere.

Here you can also swim in crystal-clear water that provides refreshment during the great heat, and a special experience comes when the sun sets and the whole landscape is immersed in golden and pink tones. Then the lakes take on an almost fairy-tale appearance. It is a perfect moment for a photograph, but also for simply enjoying the silence of nature.

In the heart of the summer season, a parking space at the viewpoint along the main road is almost impossible to find. Down by the lakes themselves, however, there are usually no crowds. Most travellers photograph the view and drive on, while those who go down to the water, sit in a boat, or cycle a loop are completely enchanted and, like us, probably think: “How is this place not far better known?”

World.title: Croatia Isn’t Facing a Fuel Shortage, But Prices Will Rise
World.content:
August the 23rd, 2026 – Croatia isn’t facing any sort of genuine fuel shortage, but experts are warning that prices will definitely rise.

Diesel shortages aren’t a realistic threat to Croatia, but prices will very likely rise again, warns energy expert Jasminko Umičević. He sees the problem in the lack of refining capacity in Europe and disruptions in supply. Poslovni reports that energy expert Jasminko Umičević spoke about the situation on the energy market, potential shortages and price movements for HRT.

Owing to disruptions on the global oil market and supply problems, concern is growing about the availability of diesel. Energy expert Jasminko Umičević believes there is no real danger of shortages in Croatia, although prices could remain high. “I don’t think there’s any real fear that shortages will occur. I believe high prices will continue, and that is the biggest problem. Regardless of the fact that the diesel market is very tight, especially across Europe. The main reason at this moment is the Strait of Hormuz and all the problems that stem from it,” says Umičević.

He also sees a problem in the structure of European refineries, which do not have sufficient capacity to produce diesel, while Europe has significantly higher consumption of this fuel than, for example, the United States. “European refineries are under-capacitated for sufficient diesel production, because the European market is a diesel market. Today we are in a situation where Europe has reduced its refining capacity by 30 percent over the last 20 years or so. Under the motto: better to import than to produce. And these are the results now,” he stresses. An additional problem for supply is the change in the sources from which Europe obtains all of its diesel.

“Previously the main source was Russia. After the sanctions everything shifted to Arab countries. Now we have a problem with the Arab countries. And recently there have been major problems, after the Ukrainian ones, with the new tactics of destroying refineries. That’s why there is no diesel. The market is tight, it’s always like that – when supply is lower, prices are higher,” he explains.

rijeka’s refinery still isn’t operating at full capacity

For Croatia in particular, the Rijeka refinery is particularly important, but its operation was briefly disrupted on Friday by a lightning strike on a substation. Umičević believes that if the problem is only with the substation, the fault could be fixed relatively quickly, but stresses that this is a situation that should not be ignored. He added that the Rijeka refinery is in any case not yet operating at full capacity because certain tests are still expected to be completed, and it should reach full capacity next year. “Especially now, the Rijeka refinery is not operating at full capacity, because the completion of some tests is still expected. Only next year will Rijeka operate at full capacity. But what is important right now is that there is production, so we aren’t dependent on imports,” he noted.

diesel prices will probably increase again

Diesel prices could rise again from next week, Umičević believes. Although the oil price has fallen in the meantime, the diesel price has remained high and continues to rise. “I think prices will rise again next week, for a very simple reason – the diesel price is rising, as is the petrol price. What is absurd, or a paradox, is that oil prices have not risen as much as the diesel price in particular,” says Umičević. “At the beginning of the Iran-US conflict in the Strait of Hormuz the oil price was around 71 dollars per barrel, and at its highest it reached 126 dollars. The diesel price then rose from around 750 to 1,300 dollars. After the situation calmed down, oil fell to around 90, and today it is around 94 dollars, while the diesel price has remained practically the same and continues to rise,” he states.

He nevertheless expects that any price increase will not be large, but notes that the final decision also depends on the Government.

“there will be enough gas, but the price of it is another thing”

As for gas, Umičević believes that the goal of filling Croatia’s Okoli storage facility to 85 percent by the 1st of October is realistic. “A month or a month and a half ago we were at around 51 percent full. Croatia has enough gas and a relatively good mix of sources – we have the LNG terminal, domestic production (which is smaller, admittedly), and diversified other sources. I think it is realistic for Croatia to reach 85 percent,” says Umičević.

He added that one of the problems is that the gas price on the futures market is lower than the current one, so storage users do not find it profitable to buy gas now at higher prices. “The key problem is that future gas prices are lower than current ones. That’s why it doesn’t pay for storage users to buy now at high prices and later sell at lower ones. However, the Government has taken certain decisions, and HEP has been given the task of filling the storage to 85 percent,” he said.

He believes there is currently no reason for concern about gas quantities, but stresses that the question of price is something else. “There will be enough gas, just as there will be enough diesel, the only question is at what price it will be sold at. Gas prices have seriously fluctuated, and after the initial summer price increase the situation has stabilised somewhat. When everything is averaged out, there should not be a significant increase in the gas price either, especially because the state already subsidises the price,” he concluded.

World.title: German Tourists Cause Fire Inside Poreč Apartment Ending With €400,000 in Damage
World.content:
August the 23rd, 2026 – German tourists have caused enormous damage after causing a fire inside a Poreč apartment. As if that wasn’t enough, he allegedly stuck his middle finger up at the owner after the act.

German tourists caused a fire in a Poreč apartment inside a family home two weeks ago, according to a police investigation. The fire destroyed almost the entire apartment, and owner Markica Kikić estimates the damage at around €400,000. Kikić has now revealed new details of the entire incident. Index reports that he claimed that some of the guests obstructed the firefighting efforts during the blaze and is also deeply dissatisfied with the police response. “The guests simply got in the way, obstructed and interfered with putting out the fire. In the meantime the police arrived and somehow managed to move them aside,” Kikić said.

“he was getting in my face and even stuck his middle finger up at me”

He claims that one of the guests still did not calm down even after the police arrived. “One of those people was sticking his middle finger under my nose and getting right in my face. The police were removing me from him instead of throwing him out. He wasn’t registered and had no right to be on my private property. The police removed me and gave them priority,” he alleged.

Kikić also claimed there were major shortcomings in the police’s handling of the whole situation. “Believe me, there were major failings on the part of the police. They gave them documents so they could fill in their own names, surnames and the rest themselves. They didn’t take them in. The police didn’t even take a statement from them. They signed and left,” he claimed. He considers the situation was serious enough to require a stricter police response.

“This is a criminal offence of endangering life and property. In such a case, as far as I as a layman know the law, the person has to be taken in and detained,” Kikić said.

he was coming back from the beach when he noticed the flames

As a reminder of previous reports on this bizarre incident, Kikić recounted that on returning from the beach he found the apartment in flames and was particularly shocked by the behaviour of the guests whom the police link to the outbreak of the fire. “They continued with their meal, toasting, raising glasses and bottles. They even got in our way while we were frantically buying hoses so we could try to put out the fire,” he said. He stated that this year’s tourist season is over for him and that he does not know whether he will manage to renovate the apartment even by next year. “For at least the next two years, I’m financially ruined,” he said.

The owner also described the sheer scale of the damage done by the fire inside the apartment. “The entire kitchen was handmade, from the highest-quality materials. All the furniture was high-quality, luxurious, paid for a lot of money. All of this is destroyed. This is a real catastrophe,” he said, adding that the apartment had been completely furnished and renovated. “An absolutely astronomical amount of money was invested in this. Everything was made of expensive materials, there were designer paintings inside with signatures,” he said.

the police say the fire started in the kitchen

The police investigation established that the fire broke out in the kitchen while a 44-year-old German citizen was preparing food.

“Due to the transfer of heat from the stove to the pan and then to the wooden structure, the fire spread to the rest of the apartment,” the police stated. Police suspect the 44-year-old woman of the criminal offence of endangering life and property by a generally dangerous act. The competent state attorney’s office will decide on further steps. The German family has in the meantime left Poreč, while the owner has been left to deal with the consequences of the fire.

Lawyer Zvonimir Matić earlier explained that the owner must first make a proper assessment of the damage, after which he can demand compensation from the German citizen in question. “The most important thing for them now is to make a quality assessment of the damage. After that they will submit a claim to the German citizen to compensate for the damage. If she does not do so, the owner will be able to file a lawsuit with the competent court in Poreč. It is important that the law is on their side,” Matić said.

“booking.com demanded that i pay for their alternative accommodation!”

Kikić had also hoped for help from the platform through which the apartment was booked, but claims Booking.com’s response further surprised him. “An hour later I received an email from the platform informing me that they had moved the guests to other accommodation, even to the most luxurious hotel, and that I had to pay for their accommodation,” he alleged. Booking.com earlier stated that they were checking the circumstances of the case and that the guest had been placed on the blocked users list while the check is ongoing.

Kikić claims that problems with the guests began the day after their arrival, when they started bringing additional people into the apartment. “When I tried to warn him, he simply arrogantly got in my face and said that he had booked the apartment and that they could do whatever they wanted in it,” he recounted. The owner estimates the damage to stand at around €400,000 in total.

World.title: Župa Dubrovačka – An Oasis Between Dubrovnik and Konavle
World.content:
August the 23rd, 2026 – Župa dubrovačka, or the Parish of Dubrovnik, is an area located between Dubrovnik and Konavle, known for its beaches, peace and distinctly less hustle and bustle.

In the extreme south of Dalmatia lies an area that is often overshadowed by its famous, world-renowned neighbour. Yet no matter how powerful the shadow of Dubrovnik may be, this region stubbornly continues to tell its own (much more relaxed) story. Putni kofer writes that that story is made up of a series of “chapters” written by the local, very old villages.

ONE OF THE MOST BEAUTIFUL PARTS OF THE DUBROVNIK RIVIERA

First, let’s get better acquainted with a few basic facts. Župa dubrovačka is located between Dubrovnik and Konavle, with the border towards the latter marked by Duboka Ljuta – a place where, according to legend, fairies used to sing noisily at night to scare away newcomers and keep all the beauty just for themselves. It spans an area of around 2,300 hectares and has about six thousand inhabitants. It’s separated from the very centre of Dubrovnik by just six kilometres and sits in a firm embrace of rolling hills on one side and the sea on the other. Župa dubrovačka is called one of the most beautiful parts of the Dubrovnik Riviera.

Its history is long and dates back to around 6000–4000 BC. One of the pieces of evidence from that time – a stone tongue-shaped chisel – is still kept in the Dubrovnik Museum. Illyrians once lived here, Greeks passed through the area, and later the Romans eventually ruled it. In the 7th century, however, Župa dubrovačka came under Dubrovnik’s control. Its natural beauty had long caught the eye of the Dubrovnik nobility, who built their summer residences there.

KUPARI – THE OLDEST TOURIST RESORT

Over time, Župa dubrovačka also grew in tourism terms, attracting visitors slowly but surely. Tourism began to develop there after the First World War and experienced a boom in the 1960s and 1970s, when a series of hotels were built in the area.

In this “tourism” sense, Kupari must be mentioned. This place is cited as the oldest tourist resort in Župa dubrovačka, and the first hotel was built there in 1920. The place got its name from the Kuparica tile factory, which operated as early as the 13th century. It is also known for one of the most famous beaches near Dubrovnik, as well as for a hotel complex that stood abandoned for a long time and has now been demolished. A new hotel is supposed to rise in its place. The only thing in the complex that was not demolished is the first hotel in the history of Župa – Hotel Grand – which is protected. It is due to be restored.

SREBRENO aND MLINI

East of Kupari lies Srebreno. This ancient fishing village, which was popular among Dubrovnik nobles who built villas there, is mentioned as early as the 13th century and is today the administrative centre of the municipality. It is also considered one of the best-known bathing spots in the area, along with Soline. That settlement got its name from the salt pans. One of the most recognisable places in Župa dubrovačka, however, is pretty little Mlini. The name was not given without reason. There used to be a series of mills in the village (mlin in Croatian), of which only one has been preserved to this day. Mlini is now widely regarded as one of the best-known tourist destinations in this compact area. It’s often referred to as one of the most beautiful settlements in Župa dubrovačka.

PLAT IS KNOWN FOR ITS BEAUTIFUL COVES

Bracodbk

Plat, another place in Župa dubrovačka, lies further south, towards Konavle. It is known for its beautiful coves and beaches, and its name Plat (formerly called Belenum) is first mentioned in 1400. It is home to several interesting little churches, for example the Church of St John, which stands on the hill above the village and where so-called mammoth spruces once grew. The thickest of them had a trunk circumference of more than two metres.

The Church of Our Lady of the Assumption was guarded by huge cypresses about 21 metres tall. The giant cypresses and spruces are gone, but near the latter church there are stećci (medieval tombstones), including one that is said to be the most beautiful in the Dubrovnik area. Finally, it is certainly worth stepping a little away from the coast itself and exploring the hinterland of Župa in general, the old villages, vineyards and olive groves, and the ancient stone houses.

World.title: Split Port: Passengers Wait in 40 Degree Heat With No Shelter From Sun
World.content:
August the 23rd, 2026 – Split Port is rapidly turning into a proverbial pizza oven as passengers have to wait in 40 degree heat with no shelter from the sun whatsoever.

At Split Port, passengers must wait to board in temperatures above 35 degrees in the shade, while on the scorching asphalt and with high humidity the perceived heat regularly exceeds 40 degrees. Lukrecija Zderic reports for Index that all of this takes place without a canopy under which people could take any form of shelter. With all the belongings they’re carrying on their journey, they must stand on the burning asphalt, exposed to the insufferable strength of the summer sun, with almost no shade available.

Parents with children, the elderly, and those waiting for the ferry try to find at least a scrap of shade under the smaller palm trees. Ferries come and go, the queues move, and passengers wait in the sun with no place to hide from the heat.

The problem becomes even greater when the catamaran or ferry is delayed and passengers don’t know exactly when it will arrive. This is precisely what happened to one of our readers, who wished to remain anonymous. With her family she had to wait in the port, in the sun and without adequate shelter, and she told Index how disappointing the whole situation was.

“It was a working day and we were supposed to travel by catamaran to Korčula. Unfortunately it was late, but that wasn’t the only problem. The biggest problem is that in Split’s port you almost have nowhere to shelter from the sun. The berths for the catamarans are far from the main, and practically the only, canopy in the port,” our interlocutor said.

“There’s often no space in the cafe or bar, and if you don’t know exactly when the catamaran will arrive or which berth it will dock at, which happens frequently, you can’t even move away to look for a shady spot. It was a heatwave, it was extremely hot, and with children it was a truly terrible experience,” the reader told us.

“if i hadn’t found shade, i’d have become unwell in the sun”

So we went to Split’s port to check whether the catamarans were late and how passengers spend their time waiting for them in the sun. Because the fact is that at the berths there is nowhere to shelter from the heat. During our arrival and the following three hours in the port, a large number of catamarans arrived and departed, and almost all of them arrived on time. The biggest delay we recorded was around ten minutes, which can hardly be called a serious delay, and it did not bother the passengers either. But what many would apparently gladly change is a simple thing – that instead of waiting on the scorching sun, they could wait for the ferry in the shade.

“It’s extremely hot, but it doesn’t bother me that much because I’m by the sea. It’s a bit inconvenient standing in the sun waiting for the ferry to Dubrovnik, so I try to find any little scrap of shade. This is more of a shadow, but it will do,” a tourist travelling to Dubrovnik told us.

“I saw that today it’s 35 degrees, and it’s the same in London, but I have to admit it’s much nicer here. Maybe because we’re on holiday, but if I hadn’t found a little shade, I would have gone crazy in the sun,” a tourist from England told us. Catamarans in Split’s City Port don’t all dock in one place; they use different berths along the operational quay. Some of them are located outside the main building of the maritime-passenger terminal. At the same time, works are underway in Split’s port on Sv. Duje Pier, where a new international maritime-passenger terminal is being built.

infrastructure upgrades – but nothing to deal with the issue of ensuring shade

Once completed, the project should take over part of the international traffic and free up Sv Duje Pier for domestic scheduled traffic, i.e. better connections between Split and the islands. But while the port infrastructure is being changed and expanded, the question remains whether the problem of protecting passengers who wait for catamarans in the open will also be solved, especially during the summer months and heatwaves.

While waiting for their catamaran, passengers try in various, and some quite inventive, ways to protect themselves from the sun. Umbrellas, caps and hats become the main defence against the scorching rays, while some hide in long sleeves and others seek refuge in the rare scraps of shade. The benches under the palm trees thus become sought-after spots, and passengers settle into every available bit of shade, however small.

“It’s very hot, we’re not used to this. We’ve put on long sleeves and are protecting ourselves with an umbrella. We hope our catamaran to Dubrovnik will arrive soon because it’s really hard to breathe here,” Japanese passengers told us. There were, however, also those who did not allow the heat to spoil their holiday mood.

“We’re from Germany and we’re only briefly in Split, and now we’re going to Hvar. We don’t have any special way of protecting ourselves from the sun; we simply try to find a little shade, although that’s not exactly easy here. We don’t want to complain – we’ve come on holiday, we’re by the sea and we’re going to one of the most beautiful islands. We won’t let a few minutes in the sun spoil our mood,” a married couple from Germany told us.

During the summer, Split Port is one of the busiest places in the city every day, yet there’s no respite from the intense heat. Back in 2024 alone, more than five million passengers passed through it on ferries and catamarans, of which more than a million on catamarans. This is a huge number of people who pass through the port every day during the season, and some of them wait for their catamarans precisely in the open, exposed to the sun and temperatures that during heatwaves exceed 35 degrees.

World.title: UK legends Morcheeba returning to Tallinn in 2027
World.content:
British electronic act Morcheeba is to return to Estonia next spring. The band last performed in Tallinn just last year.

Morcheeba, formed in rural Kent in 1995, soon gained traction after meeting vocalist Skye Edwards in London, meeting with mainstream success soon after. Morcheeba blends trip-hop, downtempo and electronic music in its work, and the band has sold more than 10 million copies across 11 studio albums released over the course of its career. Hits included "Rome Wasn't Built in a Day" and "The Sea."

The latest of these is last year's "Escape the Chaos," which will also be showcased on the concert tour coming to Tallinn.

The lineup has evolved over the years, with founder member Ross Godfrey the constant. He is currently joined by Edwards, who rejoined the band in 2012 after a split in the early 2000s.

"Escape the Chaos" took two years to work on and sees Morcheeba returning to its roots by combining electronic sounds with live instruments and trip-hop with soul, blues and psychedelia.

The 2025 gig was in Tallinn's Freedom Square, but next year's will be indoors at the Alexela Concert Hall, also in the capital, on April 20.

The date is part of a wider tour of Europe, including the Baltic states, and worldwide will take in Australia, Brazil, Canada and the U.S.

World.title: Pre‑shoots for the movie 'Ümera jõel' took place in Ida‑Virumaa
World.content:
The pre‑shoots for the historical film "Ümera jõel" ("On the Ümera River"), based on Mait Metsanurk's novel and held in Ida‑Virumaa, gave the filmmakers a sense of what the Estonian‑Latvian‑Finnish co‑production might become.

The screenwriter of "Ümera jõel," which tells of the 13th‑century fight for freedom, is Mikk Mägi, who is also the director of the film.

"There is tragedy and drama, but above all it is a story of young men who become adults through trials. It is an adventurous‑epic war film. I based the story largely on the book 'Ümera jõel' and on historical events and background," Mägi said.

The first script for the film was written by the writer and military expert Leo Kunnas, but since it diverged greatly from Mait Metsanurk's text, a new script was written at the request of the producers by Mikk Mägi. War scenes from Kunnas's script are planned to be used in the film.

According to cinematographer Rein Kotov, war films require very thorough preparation.

Filmi "Ümera jõel" võtted Aidu karjääris 2026. aasta suvel Autor/allikas: Anastassia Volkova

"There are a lot of fight scenes here – knife fights, sword fights. Fight scenes in particular require a long training and rehearsal period, and we have prepared for them for quite a while," Kotov said.

The main filming of "Ümera jõel" is planned for next summer.

"Mägiste was located 'historically,' meaning based on the book, somewhere in South Estonia, and we also plan to film in Latvia, in the hilly landscape described in the book, and additionally in Ida‑Virumaa – that is the plan at the moment," Mägi said.

The main character of the film is Vello, who grows from an outcast child into the leader of his home village, played by Ursel Tilk. During the pre‑shoots in Aidu, Ida‑Virumaa, he got a sense of what kind of film it will be.

"A week ago I still had in my head 'what, how, in what way?' meaning how we will manage all of this, but now it already feels like it will be a cool and powerful undertaking, and I think the film will be epic and impressive," Tilk said.

"Ümera jõel" is expected to reach cinemas in autumn 2028.

World.title: Ironman volunteers praised for weathering storm to support 7,500 athletes
World.content:
A total of 7,500 people, a record number, took part in Ironman events in Tallinn and Harju County, backed by volunteers who supported athletes on land and water.

Organizers have thanked the 1,500 people who volunteered their time to make the weekend's Tallinn Ironman triathlon a success.

This year's event was particularly tough due to the severe weather conditions, which left some athletes at risk of suffering from exposure. The start and finish lines were at the Unibet Arena, where facilities were set up to cater to the roughly 7,500 competitors.

The full Ironman triathlon took place Saturday, with the half-distance version (70.3) following on Sunday. However, there was little rest for some of the volunteers between the two events – they were unable to clock off until around 2 a.m., when the final finishers of the main event crossed the line (even the eventual winner was not home and dry till mid-afternoon).

Worse still, Estonia was being buffeted by storms from Saturday afternoon onward, which made the lives of competitors and volunteers alike all the tougher – even some of the tents provided for shelters came loose from their moorings in the high winds, and portable toilets blew over as well. Nonetheless, on Sunday, everyone was back on duty, and the weather cooperated this time too.

One such volunteer was Reform Party MP Pipi-Liis Siemann, whose own partner was competing.

The weather was stormy, wet and windy meaning competitors needed to warm up quickly after finishing. Source: ERR

"Fortunately, the weather today was better than we feared, so I believe everyone will make it to the finish. I'm also waiting for my husband, who is out on the course today," Siemann told "Aktuaalne kaamera."

Chief organizer Ain-Alar Juhanson said the competition simply could not have gone ahead without the 1,500 volunteers.

"I have to say, it's been an incredibly great team. In all that rain, our volunteers were sitting at the aid stations without tents, as they had blown away. They were out there in the rain for six hours serving our athletes," Juhanson noted.

The volunteers' main tasks were directing traffic, pointing athletes — many of them professional internationals — to the right places and helping them with the transition from the swimming phase to the cycling phase, and then from the cycling stage to the final marathon or half-marathon run. They also handed out medals and looked after spectators, among other jobs.

Siemann said she had for several years already served as a lifeguard at the Ironman swimming stage. This time, too, she was there on a stand-up paddleboard at Lake Raku, keeping participants safe. This was the first event where the lake, just south of the city, was used, and conditions were tough there too.

"The lifeguard's job is to keep an eye on people's lives and health, but of course we also help them stay on course. With yesterday's [Saturday's – ed.] fog, that wasn't particularly easy. People wanted to know where the next point, the next buoy was. Even today, when visibility is better, people can easily lose their sense of direction when they get fatigued. Then, even before the finish, they ask how much farther it is, and we have to motivate them and say 'come on, it's only a few hundred meters, not much more'!" Siemann recounted.

Lifeguards at the swimming stage were present on SUP boards. Source: ERR

Karoli Sõmermaa, from Paide, was another volunteer, and she managed to get a friend, Enrico Anton, to take part this year too. They also had their share of memorable moments during the stormy competition.

"One portable toilet blew over, and the athletes came inside still shivering, and they were vomiting and fainting, so it was actually very difficult to watch and you have to be emotionally prepared for that," Sõmermaa noted.

"We mostly worked indoors yesterday. When they came in, they were shivering all over, and for some of them we had to call in medics to help," Anton added.

The full Ironman was won by Frenchman Remi Conte in a time of eight hours and eight minutes, while local competitor Henry Räppo won the 70.3 event in a time of three hours 38 minutes. The first woman finisher in the full triathlon was Finland's Laura Jalasto, and Liis Kapten, an Estonian, battled hard to come third in the half-triathlon — Italy's Marta Bernardi.

World.title: Study: Laughing at a foreign‑sounding Estonian helps protect Estonian identity
World.content:
The Americanized Estonian has become a fixed stereotype in Estonian culture through which people express fear of the disappearance of the Estonian language and identity, according to a study.

Many of us have likely heard young people spice up their everyday speech with English expressions or have smirked at a foreign‑accented Estonian speaker. A new study shows that such an Americanized Estonian is not just a random phenomenon but a firmly rooted character in our culture. Through this figure, society deals with the fear that the Estonian language and identity may disappear.

This conclusion was reached by University of Tartu doctoral student Martin Nõmm. He examined Estonian cultural texts from 1950s diaspora literature to contemporary media and social networks.

The analysis highlighted that the comic stereotype has changed over time but has preserved its core. Already in decades‑old diaspora plays and films, young people longing for American‑style wealth were depicted. They spoke a mixed English‑Estonian language known as Estonglish.

In re‑independent Estonia, symbols of "Mickey‑Mousing" include the broad‑stroked character Thor‑Björn Margna from the TV series "Õnne 13" or the naive social‑media persona "Älice megaa põnev elu."

It also emerged that this image is used as a political weapon. For example, media and parody shows repeatedly emphasized former president Toomas Hendrik Ilves's foreign‑sounding accent. He was even portrayed once with Mickey Mouse ears.

According to the researcher, the explanation lies in social dynamics and superiority humor. When two cultural spheres collide, dissonance arises, and laughing at a foreign‑sounding Estonian becomes a kind of defense mechanism. It helps locals strengthen their sense of belonging and provides support in a situation where Western pop culture and the English language tend to push in too strongly.

The research results were published in the journal Keel ja Kirjandus.

World.title: 87 years since Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact marked with memorial events across Estonia
World.content:
Sunday marked 87 years since the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact was signed. The agreement, between the Soviet Union and Nazi Germany, paved the way for Estonia's over 50 years of occupation.

The pact's secret protocols carved up Central and Eastern Europe into Nazi German and Soviet spheres of influence, with Estonia falling under the latter category.

In Tallinn, the anniversary was marked with a public meeting in Hirvepark, a key location in the Singing Revolution of the late 1980s which led to the restoration of Estonia's independence. A remembrance ceremony at the Memorial to the Victims of Communism in Tallinn was also held.

The day is marked not only in Estonia but also Europe-wide, particularly in those countries most affected by the pact, and against the backdrop of the war on Ukraine conducted by the Soviet Union's successor state, the Russian Federation.

Justice Minister Liisa Pakosta (Eesti 200) said in her speech that Sunday's European Day of Remembrance for Victims of Totalitarian and Authoritarian Regimes is primarily observed by countries that suffered under both German and Soviet occupations.

"Elsewhere, there seems to be a sense that the matter was settled with the Nuremberg trials, but in reality that was not the case. One side was punished and the other went unpunished. The war in Ukraine today is a continuation of that impunity," Pakosta said.

The MRP memorial service in the Maarjamäe district of Tallinn. Source: ERR

Karl Erik Kirss of the Estonian school student councils' union said the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact (MRP) and the events that followed it also directly concern young people today, born many decades later.

"Such tragic historical events, which led to what happened in the 20th century, still affect us today. We can still see the remnants of the Soviet era nowadays," Kirss said.

Anne Eenpalu, board chair of Tallinn Memento, called it important to preserve the Estonian language. Everyone who has settled, or intends to settle, in Estonia should also learn the language to the best of their ability.

"I, who was born in Siberia into a family of deportees, am highly grateful that I am in my free Estonian state, and I love my Estonian language. Every nationality has its own ethnic culture, its own customs and its own food traditions, and these must be respected, but in a free country, people must know the language of that country," Eenpalu said.

Memorial service held in Viljandi County

Also on Sunday, a memorial service for victims of communism and Nazism in Pilistvere, Viljandi County, was attended by around 200 people.

The Estonian Memento Union (Eesti Memento liit) and the local Pilistvere congregation jointly held the service, which commemorated MRP Memorial Day too.

Speeches were given at Pilistvere, but people were also able to relate their own personal experiences, including those who were alive at the time of the Siberian deportation of Estonians and were caught up in that atrocity.

"We were given half an hour, and then the journey to Siberia began. My father was so frightened, he did not know what to do about it; he had never harmed anyone. They used to say that children and women would not be deported, but everything turned out the reverse," Viivi Lemberpuu-Tootmaa, one victim of the March 1949 deportation, told "Aktuaalne kaamera."

Many never returned to their homeland – commemorating their memory is a big part of the Estonian Memento Union's remit.

"Our relatives – fathers, mothers, grandfathers, grandmothers – have often remained in a foreign land, where they have neither a cross nor a stone. And in 1988, stones symbolizing release from sorrow began to be brought here. So it is our sacred duty to return here again," said Arnold Aljase, board chair of the Estonian Memento Union.

Pilistvere has a noted occupation memorial site as well as war memorials.

An amendment to the Russian Federation's constitution made in 2020 stated that it is the successor to the Soviet Union.

World.title: Artists donate 124 works for emergency auction after €700,000 fraud loss
World.content:
The Estonian Artists' Association (EKL), together with an expert commission consisting of art historians, critics and art‑market specialists, selected the works that will go to an emergency auction to partially cover the financial damage caused by a fraud scheme. The auction will also include 124 newly donated works from artists.

In addition to the donated works, pieces from the Artists' Association art collection will go under the hammer. These works were mainly acquired from well‑known Estonian authors who have exhibited at spring and autumn exhibitions. When making the selection, the working group considered both recent developments in the art market and the principle of preserving the substantive integrity of the union's art collection, which reflects the diversity of Estonian art life. The entire collection will not be auctioned.

At least one valuable work from each author will remain in the EKL collection, and several works from many artists, said EKL vice president Tüüne‑Kristin Vaikla. Works that speak about the artists and art life itself will remain untouched.

"We are organizing the auction as openly as possible: all art enthusiasts can participate, either on site at the ARS Art City or online. The works that find new owners at the auction will not disappear from public view – a clause will be added to the purchase agreement allowing the works to be exhibited at future shows. This way, Estonia's art heritage remains accessible even after the sale," Vaikla added.

Artists donated 124 works. Artist Jaanus Samma, who coordinated the arrival of the works, said that the donations show that artists stand together and want to contribute to the union.

"Difficulties have a unifying effect; I have personally experienced this over the past weeks," he said. "Artists bring in works, ask how things are going, wish success and offer help. Preparing the auction has been very exciting; I have met many artists, visited studios and felt a sense of community."

Among the works at the auction are pieces by Jüri Arrak, Enn Põldroos, Tiit Pääsuke, Leonhard Lapin, Jüri Kask, Olev Subbi and Mari Kurismaa.

Authors of works sold from the union's collection will receive five percent of the sales revenue, in line with good secondary‑market practice. Authors of newly donated works will receive 15 percent.

The selection of works from the EKL collection for the auction was made by a working group consisting of: Harry Liivrand (EKL council representative, art historian and art‑market expert), Jaanus Samma (artist, EKL council and Art Infrastructure Council member), Liina Linsi (Art Infrastructure Council member), Tiina Määrmann (art‑market expert), Eero Epner (art historian), Kai Lobjakas (design and applied arts expert), Elnara Taidre (art historian and critic), Reigo Kuivjõgi (Estonian Art Auctions), Ain Kaldra (Estonian Art Auctions), Maarin Ektermann (EKL president) and Tüüne‑Kristin Vaikla (EKL vice president).

A fixed number of works can be put up for sale each day of the three‑day auction, which set clear limits for the selection. Works that did not make it into the selection this time will be sold at a separate exhibition sale in EKL galleries at the end of the year.

EKL is currently preparing descriptions and digital versions of the works going to auction, together with experts. These will be used in the auction's online environment and in hall and other presentation texts. After that, the full list of works and starting prices will be published.

The auction will take place from 8–10 October at the ARS Art City. The auction works can be viewed more closely at an exhibition opening on 18 September at the Art City.

On 15 May, EKL discovered that nearly €700,000 had been transferred out of the union's bank accounts through a criminal fraud scheme. The perpetrators gained access to EKL's bank accounts and transferred the money abroad under the guise of salary payments. The EKL council approved the board's proposal to take out a loan to cover the resulting costs, organize an emergency art auction and sell real estate.

World.title: 75 MPs nominate justice chancellor as presidential candidate
World.content:
Seventy-five members of the Riigikogu registered Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise as an official presidential candidate on Monday as the nomination period draws to a close.

Estonia's president is elected by the Riigikogu, and a candidate must be put forward by MPs. At least 68 votes of a potential 101 are needed to elect the next head of state.

Madise is in the middle of her second seven-year term as chancellor of justice and has the support of coalition parties Reform and Eesti 200, as well as opposition parties Isamaa and SDE.

On Monday morning, MPs from the four party factions handed in 75 signatures in support of Madise and registered her as an official candidate at 11 a.m.

It was initially reported that Madise had the support of 74 candidates, but Isamaa's Andres Metsoja later added his signature to the list.

MPs from EKRE and Center did not support Madise's nomination, and neither did SDE's Züleyxa Izmailova not Isamaa's Priit Sibul, or Helir-Valdor Seeder.

Ülle Madise. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

MPs from the Eesti 200, Isamaa, Reform and SDE factions submitted Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise as a candidate for the presidential election on August 24, 2026. Source: Iris Tähema/ERR

Members of the Riigikogu who signed the nomination of Madise are listed below:

Jaak Aab, Annely Akkermann, Yoko Alender, Anti Allas, Lea Danilson-Järg, Enn Eesmaa, Ants Frosch, Andre Hanimägi, Andres Metsoja, Anti Haugas, Lauri Hussar, Diana Ingerainen, Jüri Jaanson, Toomas Järveoja, Maria Jufereva-Skuratovski, Mario Kadastik, Raimond Kaljulaid, Madis Kallas, Jaanus Karilaid, Ester Karuse, Liina Kersna, Helmen Kütt, Tanel Kiik, Signe Kivi, Ando Kiviberg, Toomas Kivimägi, Mait Klaassen, Aivar Kokk, Eerik-Niiles Kross, Urmas Kruuse, Katrin Kuusemäe, Kalle Laanet, Hanah Lahe, Alar Laneman, Maris Lauri, Mihkel Lees, Irja Lutsar, Tõnis Lukas, Lauri Läänemets, Mart Maastik, Tiit Maran, Eero Merilind, Marko Mihkelson, Tõnis Mölder, Heljo Pikhof, Õnne Pillak, Henn Põlluaas, Mati Raidma, Juku-Kalle Raid, Reili Rand, Valdo Randpere, Marek Reinaas, Urmas Reinsalu, Signe Riisalo, Maido Ruusmann, Stig Rästa, Kersti Sarapuu, Andrus Seeme, Pipi-Liis Siemann, Riina Sikkut, Timo Suslov, Margit Sutrop, Aivar Sõerd, Kadri Tali, Peeter Tali, Tarmo Tamm, Tanel Tein, Urve Tiidus, Madis Timpson, Vilja Toomast, Toomas Uibo, Kristo Enn Vaga, Luisa Värk, Mart Võrklaev, Kristina Šmigun-Vähi.

World.title: Fewer apartments on rental market ahead of new academic year
World.content:
The rental market has picked up as autumn and the start of the school year approach, but the number of available living spaces has decreased by almost 10 percent this year and prices have risen.

There is just over a week left until the new academic year starts, which means thousands of students have once again set the rental market buzzing. Apartments in prefabricated buildings and smaller wooden houses are in high demand.

However, there are around 10 percent fewer apartments on offer this year than last year. The Uus Maa real estate agency has observed a similar situation.

"While demand was at roughly the same level, supply this year was 7 percent lower compared with 2025. Those 7 percent have most likely started renting out their apartments on a short-term basis," Uus Maa Pro real estate agent Karl-Villiam Vaserik told Sunday's "Aktuaalne kaamera."

Demand has pushed up apartment prices. The average rent for a one- or two-room apartment is currently between €400–650 a month, depending on its condition and location.

"For a student, that €400–650 is quite a significant sum, especially in the first years when the student is not working. It is not very easy to take that out of the parents' wallet either. You also have to add money for food and other expenses," said Luminor chief economist Lenno Uusküla.

He said prices have risen "because they can be raised."

"Apparently there are relatively few offers. On the other hand, if you look at Estonian consumer confidence, it has improved. At the beginning of the year, those earning above the median wage took home more money as a result of the income tax change," Uusküla said.

The most desirable districts of the capital for students are the city center, Põhja-Tallinn and Mustamäe, which are closest to the universities.

There is also another, cheaper option on the table – renting accommodation in a dormitory.

"The cheapest option is €161 a month, a bed in a double room. Everything is already included in the price," said Jaak Kääp, head of Tallinn University of Technology's student village.

However, a brand new dormitory at TalTech has a price tag of €440 a month, which includes all additional costs. There are 150 students on the waiting list.

"In previous years, we practically had no one waiting at all; this year, suddenly, we do," Kääp said.

For those currently without accommodation, more options should become available on the rental market again in a few months, and prices should also come down slightly.
