World.title: 'Vector for antisemitism' platformed on media network that got government grant
World.content:
A Sydney-based podcast network that received federal grant funding to support social cohesion platformed a known conspiracy theorist who was deported and received a lifetime ban from Australia, an inquiry has heard.

The Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion was told on Monday that American livestreamer Sneako, whose real name is Nicolas Kenn De Balinthazy, was deported from Australia in May after initially being granted a visa.

During his visit, Sneako was interviewed by OnePath Network, an Australian Islamic-themed podcast based in Sydney that was established in 2014.

The Anti-Defamation League, an organisation that combats antisemitism, describes Sneako as "one of the most prominent vectors for antisemitism, white supremacy, and misogyny in the manosphere" with an audience of millions.

Sneako was deported from Australia in May. (Supplied: OnePath Network)

It said his following was predominantly made up of men and boys, and that his extremist and antisemitic content had been amplified across YouTube, TikTok and Instagram.

The commission heard Sneako had previously been banned from YouTube, Twitch (an interactive livestreaming service) and TikTok.

$308,000 grant for podcast network

Public documents show OnePath Network's parent organisation, OPN Media Limited, received a $308,000 grant from the Department of Home Affairs under the independent multicultural media transformation and sustainability program.

The funding is designed to support social cohesion and the sustainability of independent multicultural media outlets.

Department of Home Affairs secretary Stephanie Foster was shown a screenshot of the grant issued to OnePath Network during Monday's hearing.

"Would you agree that it's an entirely inappropriate use of grant money to platform Sneako, who is a person who received a lifetime ban from entering this country because of views he's expressed publicly?," counsel representing various Jewish bodies, Nicholas Bender SC, put to Ms Foster.

Ms Foster said she was unaware of the screenshot.

"We will always, when information is provided to us, investigate its validity and it's appropriateness," she said.

In response to the funding allocation, a spokesperson for OnePath Network said in a statement that OPN Media was among 60 recipients of the grants scheme.

"OPN Media takes the work of the Royal Commission and its editorial responsibilities seriously," it said.

"Questions put to a witness during a hearing are not findings made by the Commission."

The OnePath interview with Sneako was titled, 'Who really is Sneako? The Manosphere, Islam and Israel' and was published in June.

The interview covered Sneako's rise to fame, his conversion to Islam, his time with Kanye West and his departure from the manosphere.

"Just based on that information, that raises a very substantial concern that this grantee is acting inappropriately, doesn't it?," Mr Bender SC asked. "As I said, we will always when we receive information that would suggest that the grantee was acting inappropriately investigate that," Ms Foster answered. "I'm reluctant to say anymore at this stage so I don't prejudice that process."

Sneako's visa cancelled

Sneako's visa was cancelled, and he was deported from Australia in May after media reporting about his visit.

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said at the time that Sneako would never be allowed to return to Australia.

"Our government has made it very clear we will use every power available to us to protect our community from people coming to this country to spread hatred," Mr Burke told News 24, formerly Sky.

Mr Burke has said that Sneako would never be allowed back into Australia. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

The inquiry heard that, three weeks before Sneako's arrival in Australia, he led a crowd in a chant invoking violence against Jews and had published material online presenting Chabad as a criminal conspiracy.

The Anti-Defamation League has documented a history of antisemitic conspiracy theories and Holocaust denial by Sneako, including his participation in an antisemitic chant in New York in April 2026.

Mr Bender SC asked Ms Foster whether Sneako should have been granted a visa in the first place.

"The decision-maker would have assessed the facts in front of them, and if the facts were identical to those that led to the cancellation of the visa, then it's not unreasonable to suggest that decision-maker would've made that decision in the first instance," she said.

"But without the facts I can't assume any of that."

Mr Bender pressed Ms Foster further.

"Do you agree that somebody who had done those things, according to the department's policies, should not be granted a visa?," Mr Bender put to Ms Foster.

Ms Foster would not be drawn on the matter.

"I'm just not able to make those assumptions," she said.

"If we have information which would preclude someone from being issued a visa based on our act then we would not have issued the visa."

Addressing antisemitism claims

During the OnePath interview, Sneako was asked about previous antisemitic comments he had made.

"According to Zionists, they'll say anyone who is critical of Israeli is antisemite," he said.

The statement from OPN Media also stressed that a disclaimer posted on its YouTube channel, and read out by the presenter prior to the interview, stated that it does not invite guests onto its platform because it agrees with everything they have "ever said or done".

"Having someone on should never be read as a blanket endorsement of all their views," it said.

"As a Muslim organisation, we reject all forms of hate speech based on race, ethnicity, or religion, including anti-Semitism and any language that mocks or trivialises the suffering of any community from past tragedies.

"At the same time, we firmly reject any attempt to conflate anti-Semitism with legitimate criticism of Israeli state policy, and we reject the weaponisation of that term to silence those speaking out against genocide."

A Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory by the UN Human Rights Council found that genocide was occurring in Gaza, but Israel has denied the allegations against it.

World.title: Specialist ship arrives to cart SpaceX rocket from Christmas Island
World.content:
Like a certain extraterrestrial, SpaceX's Starship 40 is set to depart its adopted safe harbour of Christmas Island and head for home.

But, far from Hollywood special effects, a highly specialised watercraft is helping it make the 17,000 kilometre journey back to Starbase, Texas.

The Forte docked within sight of Starship 40 on Sunday. (Supplied: Svyatoslav Shanygin)

The Forte is a heavy-lift, semi submersible cargo carrier sailing beneath a Maltese flag.

The ABC tracked the vessel using publicly available marine traffic data from Indonesia to Christmas Island's Flying Fish Cove, where it docked late on Sunday evening.

The Forte has anchored within a few hundred metres of Starship 40, where it will sink its stern to load the floating 52-metre-long rocket directly from the water.

Islander Lisa Preston described the spectacle as awe-inspiring.

"It's quite surreal going past it on a boat and having a look at this rocket," she said.

"Then we've, as humans beings, designed this other piece of machinery that can pull that out of the ocean and semi-submerge and float itself again and sail off with the rocket.

" I've been living here nearly 30 years and this will make one of the top 10 experiences. "

It is believed the Forte is making final preparations to load the wayward space shuttle. (Supplied: Lisa Preston)

Christmas Island Tourism Association chair David Watchorn headed out before sunrise to watch the Forte up close, calling it the biggest vessel he had ever seen at Christmas Island.

"It's huge, it pales [other ships] in significance," Mr Watchorn said.

Sad farewell

The rocket's presence on the remote Australian territory has caused lots of excitement in the tight-knit island community, especially among its youngest residents.

George says he had "so many books about planets", then a rocket landed in his backyard. (Supplied)

Space enthusiast George Pride, age 9, said it was something he and his schoolmates would never forget.

"I went like one metre away from it," he said.

" It's massive, it's very interesting and you can see all the heat shields. "

Ellyse, 10, called the past week a "once in a life" opportunity. (Supplied)

Ellyse Ingwersen, age 10, said she would be sad to see it go.

"It was a really cool spaceship, I think it's like a once in a life opportunity."

Retrieved for analysis

The recovery mission comes almost a week after Starship 40 was towed to Christmas Island, more than 1,500 kilometres off Western Australia's coast.

The ship, described by SpaceX as the upper-stage attached to the world's most powerful booster, made a controlled touchdown in the Indian Ocean on July 24.

SpaceX rocket splashes down off Christmas Island A SpaceX rocket is being towed off Christmas Island after landing in the Indian Ocean in an unusual spectacle for locals.

It then spent 24 days at sea as crews from the mainland battled rough weather and delays.

At the time, a spokesperson for the Australian Space Agency confirmed the federal government was assisting SpaceX with its efforts.

During an earnings call earlier this month, SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk said the flight of Starship 40 demonstrated the "core capabilities" of an orbital mission and return to Starbase for "catch".

It is expected to return to Texas for analysis by engineers.

The company hopes to launch, catch, and reuse its rockets going forward, with last month's soft splashdown a key test of its performance.

David Gozzard, a senior research fellow at the University of Western Australia, said the retrieval would yield crucial data.

"It's going to help design future starships, so that when they make them reusable and are flying each one again and again … they will be a much more reliable and robust product," he said.

Loading...

Yet in a post to his X account last week, Mr Musk admitted a catch attempt on dry land was still some way off.

"If there had been a tower out to sea where we practised landing the ship, it would have been caught," he wrote.

"First reflight (sic) of the ship will be either [the] end of this year or early next.

" That will be a fork in the road of history for consciousness reaching the stars. "

World.title: How a personal pitch from the PNG prime minister helped seal Manu’s NRL return
World.content:
Updated SportNRLNRL 2026 How a personal pitch from the PNG prime minister helped seal Manu’s NRL return Dan Walsh Updated August 24, 2026 — 9:30pm ,first published August 24, 2026 — 7:32am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A personal sales pitch from Papua New Guinea Prime Minister James Marape helped seal Joey Manu’s return to rugby league, which is expected to begin with a short-term 2027 deal at an NRL rival before he takes up a two-year deal with the PNG Chiefs from 2028. The Kiwi international’s long-touted signing with the expansion franchise was confirmed on Monday morning. Loading Manu has already been offered to several NRL clubs as a potential short-term signing for the back half of 2027 once he completes the final year of his estimated €1 million ($1.6 million) contract with French rugby outfit Racing 92. He will be 31 by the time he links with PNG for their first pre-season late next year, and the Chiefs can see an advantage in Manu joining an NRL rival as a pre-June 30 signing, as was raised by the Warriors earlier this season.



Manu ultimately knocked back that approach to ensure he didn’t jeopardise his lucrative rugby deal. But his appeal and pedigree as a potential game-breaker in next year’s title race have been noted at several clubs spoken to by this masthead on Monday after his PNG move was announced. A $300,000 sign-on figure for a three-month return was reported earlier this year as a fair market value, according to the NRL salary cap auditor for the Kiwi star; it would equate to a $1.2 million salary. Former Rooster Joey Manu and his family – pictured at Port Moresby airport – toured the Chiefs facilities earlier this year. His signature comes as the Chiefs continue to reshape a volatile player market, with Hudson Young to begin formal talks with PNG next month despite Canberra tabling him a record $3.3 million, three-year extension offer – the richest deal in the club’s history. The Chiefs are also in talks with Titans star AJ Brimson after he was given permission to explore an early exit from the Gold Coast.



Speaking from France after committing to PNG as their seventh signing, Manu said Marape’s passion for bringing an NRL side to the wider Pacific region had helped sway him, while he had also been impressed by the Chiefs’ Port Moresby facilities. “Talking to the [PNG] prime minister, how passionate he was about making it not just a Papua New Guinea team but making it a Pacific team, and trying to get the Pacific nations behind this team, I think it’s going to be special,” Manu said. Joey Manu left the NRL as one of the best players in the game. NRL Imagery “I’m a really proud Cook Island and Māori man, and I know my family’s real proud back in Tokoroa in New Zealand – and also in the Cook Islands, too. “There’s so much talent in the Pacific Islands and rugby league is taking over the islands, so it’s really cool to have sort of a Pacific team.”



The Australian government’s much-discussed $600 million funding package around the club sets aside as much as $350 million in rugby league pathways development programs across PNG, Fiji, Samoa and Tonga, according to a Senate estimates committee hearing held last year. Related Article Analysis

NRL 2026 Good luck, NRL rivals. The Warriors can now stay in NZ until grand final week Manu looms as a potential fullback option given he regularly wore the No.1 for New Zealand at Test level. A rugby league return at centre – where he was widely regarded as the best in the game throughout a 181-game career with the Roosters – may be more suitable, though, given his age and the added running required of fullbacks under the NRL’s new set-restart rules. “It’s just been a few years now since I’ve been out of the game, and I still watch a few games when I can,” Manu said.



“You miss certain things when you’re watching, and I’m just grateful that I get to come back and play. Rugby league is a special game for myself and to come back and play in the NRL is very special.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: A piece o’ cord for bouncers
World.content:
“Adding to the ridiculous practice of establishments requiring a tie for entry (C8), in the late ’60s I was denied entry to the Chatswood Charles Hotel. They stated I needed a tie,” says Max Redmayne of Drummoyne. “My response was to take a shoelace and create a bow tie, and yes, that was acceptable, which points to the ludicrous practice.”

“During the 1997 Australian Professional Sumo Tour I was deputised by Wide World of Sports to take two sumo wrestlers to Eagle Farm racecourse for a day out and to present the trophy for the main race,” writes Katrina Watts of Murwillumbah. “They wore traditional cotton yukata (kimono) and zori (straw sandals). As they were greeted and ushered into the members enclosure I heard a dapper gent comment, ‘Just a minute, those two men can’t come in here. They are in dresses, have no ties and are wearing thongs!’”

Of course there are some establishments that secede from a typical dress code, as evidenced by Denis O’Calahan of Auckland, New Zealand: “In 1976, I was in Dallas, Texas, for training. They took us out to a restaurant called The Traildust where the sign on the door said ‘No Neckties’. If anyone tried to enter wearing a tie, a waiter would come out with a huge pair of scissors and cut it off. The walls were decorated with hundreds of the cut-off ties.”

James White of Beverage (Vic) reckons the media have blown the gig: “Whose cage do I rattle to get the news out that last weekend, Boyd Excell won his eighth consecutive title at the Four-in-Hand World Championship in Europe? He is a spectacular competitor in a sport that is spectacular But nothing in the news.”

“In the early 1970s, I was refused admission to Eastern Suburbs Leagues Club due to my hair being over my collar,” recalls Geoff Genford of Hurlstone Park.“I didn’t feel so bad when I read that hirsute star player and former rugby union international Russell Fairfax was taken into the club to sign his contract via the tradesman’s entrance.” Margaret Bellingham Holle of Woollahra remembers it, too.

World.title: ‘Could see myself sitting here’: One Nation MP Farley gatecrashes Liberal meeting
World.content:
One Nation MP David Farley has fuelled speculation about his future in Pauline Hanson’s party after accidentally walking into a private meeting of more than 20 Liberal MPs – then telling them he could see himself sitting with them. The extraordinary encounter happened in Parliament House last Wednesday when Farley wandered into a regular meeting of Liberal MPs from marginal seats. Several Liberals present said the Farrer MP took a while to realise he was in the wrong room before turning to leave. Farrer MP David Farley during his swearing-in on June 2. Alex Ellinghausen “I could see myself sitting here,” Farley told the MPs, before walking out. “We were all taken aback, to be honest,” one Liberal MP said. “It was a very loose thing to say.”



Farley confirmed the incident on Monday, but portrayed it as an off-the-cuff joke after accidentally entering the room. Editor's pick Immigration Every morning, a grandmother wakes 11 children. Their parents are thousands of kilometres away He said the Liberal MPs had a “who-hit-John” look on their faces, silent with their mouths open, before he “filled the empty space with my quip” and left. Liberal MP Andrew Hastie said Farley was currently a member of One Nation “but certainly let’s see what the future holds”. “He’s a decent fellow, I’ve met him a couple of times,” Hastie told ABC’s 7.30.



The remark comes at an awkward time for One Nation, with Farley again publicly at odds with Hanson over one of the party’s central political issues. The Farrer MP told ABC’s Insiders that while One Nation wanted to reduce net overseas migration to 130,000, it would allow another 100,000 migrant workers through skilled visas, backpacker programs and the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility scheme. That would put the effective number at about 230,000 – broadly in line with Labor’s forecast of 225,000 by 2027–28. Hanson moved quickly to reject Farley’s interpretation, insisting One Nation’s policy was to cut net overseas migration to 130,000, with some short-term agricultural workers excluded from the official measure. One Nation leader Pauline Hanson and Farley, pictured on May 13, don’t see eye to eye on the party’s net overseas migration figure. Alex Ellinghausen



One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce was then sent out to clean up the mess, telling Sunrise that Farley had simply got it wrong. “Show me a political career where people haven’t made a mistake, and I’ll show you a person who’s not told the truth.” Joyce said One Nation had seemingly raised the matter with Farley but refused to elaborate. “Oh, look, I’m not going to throw anybody under a bus,” he said. “When people are new in parliament, they can sometimes get things incorrect, and that’s what happens. God knows I’ve done it enough.” “I think [Farley] would have been offended by [One Nation’s head of operations] James Ashby going on News24 last night with a mop and essentially mocking what I thought were his thoughtful contributions on [ABC’s] Insiders yesterday,” Hastie said.



Hastie was referring to Ashby’s appearance on News24 on Sunday night where he brandished a mop and clarified One Nation’s migration policies, stating he’d spoken to Farley and that “people make mistakes”. “For a new member of parliament, it’s always difficult getting your head around those [net overseas migration] numbers,” Ashby said. Farley’s comments were also savaged by online news site One News Australia, which branded his appearance a “rookie blunder” and claimed his “clueless” performance had given Labor an “escape route” from its migration policy. The criticism is notable given One News Australia’s origins as the One Nation Supporters Network before it was rebranded as a news organisation. The site and the party say they have no affiliation, although its coverage is strongly pro-One Nation and Hanson. Farley was previously counselled by Hanson during the Farrer byelection campaign after he agreed a net migration figure of 306,000 last year was “probably not” too many.



The pair also exchanged harsh words after it was revealed that he’d previously tried to seek preselection with Labor for the seat and not informed anyone within One Nation before it was revealed by this masthead. Related Article Immigration Pauline Hanson’s deleted post deepens One Nation’s migration muddle Farley has already shown he is prepared to depart from Hanson’s position in the parliament. Last week he voted with the Coalition on an amendment to Labor’s wagering legislation, despite Hanson having previously committed to supporting the government’s ban on foreign matched lotteries. His growing independence is being watched closely by Coalition MPs, particularly given his conservative and agricultural background.



Sources in the Coalition said Opposition Leader Angus Taylor knew Farley from his time as an agribusiness leader and could potentially use the relationship to court him in future, although there are no immediate plans to do so. “He is a Nat or a country Liberal, not a populist,” one Liberal MP said. Farley told Insiders he came from the conservative LNP tradition, joined the Nationals after returning to Farrer and later explored joining Labor and running as an independent. He ultimately chose One Nation because he said it offered the “political courage” and “tenacity” he wanted. “I have the full support of the party to pursue what I’m doing, especially for Farrer,” he said. World.title: ‘Unite behind our club’: Powerbroker’s call for peace as McVeigh appointed Essendon coach
World.content:
Updated SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘Unite behind our club’: Powerbroker’s call for peace as McVeigh appointed Essendon coach Jake Niall and and Peter Ryan Updated August 24, 2026 — 8:12pm ,first published 6:11pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Former Essendon president Lindsay Tanner has urged the club’s supporters to unite behind the club following the appointment of Mark McVeigh as the Bombers’ new coach. In a comment made before the board ratified McVeigh’s appointment Tanner, who led the club as president from 2016 until 2020, called for unity and highlighted the thorough process that Essendon had run in searching for a replacement for Brad Scott. Mark McVeigh will leave his role as an assistant coach at the Swans for the Bombers’ top job. AFL Photos “I urge all Bombers supporters to unite behind our club, team and new coach,” Tanner said, in a statement to this masthead. “The club has run a rigorous and exhaustive coach appointment process and now we must all bond together to drive the Bombers back up the ladder.”



Tanner’s appeal for unity was crafted before it was reported that McVeigh was to make a presentation to the full board and was made irrespective of which of the final four candidates was hired. The comments of the former federal finance minister followed widespread debate and division within Essendon’s fan base, especially on the question of whether ex-coach and champion James Hird should return as coach. Former Essendon president Lindsay Tanner. Darrian Traynor Hird, who expressed disappointment at missing out on a third stint as Essendon coach, is a longstanding friend of McVeigh. He congratulated McVeigh saying he was proud of his friend.



“From a personal point of view though, it’s very disappointing,” Hird said on Nine’s Footy Furnace. “Yeah, I’m disappointed, put my heart and soul into the effort, but obviously fell short and that’s the way it goes.” Loading Long-time member Brett Crabtree had threatened to force a board spill if Hird was not appointed. Scott’s tenure was destabilised from the beginning when legendary coach Kevin Sheedy, who was on the board when Scott was appointed, said Hird was his preferred choice. Tanner, who led the club through the crisis of the year-long suspensions of the then 34 current and former players for doping offences by the Court of Arbitration for Sport, is a good friend of his predecessor, the billionaire businessman Paul Little, a strong supporter of Hird in his bid to return as senior coach.



McVeigh, who has signed a three-year deal, beat Hird, Jaymie Graham and Murray Davis to the job. In a message to Essendon fans he declared: “It’s so good to be home.” The former Bomber was the only candidate to make a final presentation to the board. He will relinquish his role as a Sydney assistant coach as the Swans try to resurrect their campaign following the club-imposed, season-ending suspensions to Isaac Heeney, Riley Bice, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey and James Jordon. Mark McVeigh coached against his former club and potential future employers on Sunday. Getty Images “We’re not looking backwards, we’re building the next great era of this football club. That’s not built on promises. It’s built on our standards, our actions and the work we put in every single day,” McVeigh said in a statement. “There’s genuine talent on this list, particularly in the emerging group, but talent alone doesn’t get you where you want to go. Our job is high standards, real connection, and total clarity on how we want to play and what it means to pull on the red and black. What excites me is what this group can become together. Our job as coaches is to build an environment that gives them every chance to get there.



“I want us to be brave. Aggressive with the ball, relentless without it, and a defensive system our players trust. When people watch Essendon play, there should be no confusion about what we stand for. Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 Butters declares he’s leaving Port, but he won’t get to Collingwood. Suns spearhead also on the move “Pre-season will be demanding. We’re establishing our standards from day one, physically, mentally, technically. There’ll be a real emphasis on competing hard and building our game model together, so every player knows exactly what’s expected of them before a ball is bounced. “I can’t wait to get started.” Dons president Andrew Welsh said the board’s decision to appoint McVeigh was unanimous.



“We are building the next successful era for Essendon, with a view to playing finals, winning finals and competing for premierships. Mark is the best coach to take us forward to achieve that,” Welsh said. “Mark was clearly the best candidate for what this role demands. He’s developed emerging talent throughout his coaching career, and he connects with younger players in a way that matters for a list at our stage. His game plan is built for the modern game, quick ball movement, adaptable structures, and it’s suited to where this competition is heading. Related Article AFL Briefing

AFL 2026 Why the AFL CEO had a public crack at Dogs star Ed Richards “He’s coached at multiple high-performing clubs and played and coached under high-performing coaches, so he knows exactly what it takes to build a winning environment. Everything he presented to us aligned with the strategy this board has already set. We weighed every candidate against what this role actually demands, and Mark was the clear standout.” McVeigh played 232 matches at Essendon after being chosen with pick No.9 in the 1998 national draft. After retiring in 2012 he moved back to NSW where he became an assistant coach at the Giants, and served as the club’s interim coach after Leon Cameron stood down in 2022.



He coached 13 matches for four wins with his former teammates James Hird and Dean Solomon in the coaches’ box alongside him. He then moved to the Sydney Swans, where he coached as an assistant under John Longmire and Dean Cox. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Pressing need for private boys schools to change entrenched hierarchy
World.content:
LifestyleGenderPrivate schools Editorial Pressing need for private boys schools to change entrenched hierarchy The Herald's View Editorial August 24, 2026 — 8:00pm

August 24, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The continuing failure by Sydney’s high-fee private boys schools to boost gender equality on their boards is under scrutiny amid renewed concerns about how a mix of privilege and concentrated masculinity affects schools’ culture. There have long been calls for all-male schools to show greater leadership on gender issues. These intensified in 2021, when 22-year-old former Kambala student Chanel Contos delivered a disturbing list of allegations from young women who said they had been sexually harassed or assaulted during high school or shortly after by young men who attended nearby Sydney private boys schools. Sydney woman Chanel Contos organised a petition in 2021 that prompted hundreds of women to share graphic stories about being violated by their male peers at private schools. Illustration by Michael Howard Contos’ focus was consent education, which is now a feature of the curriculum from kindergarten to year 10. Schools can work on boys’ perception of women in other ways, too, and one of them is embracing female leadership.



Yet a new Herald analysis shows men still outnumber women on the governing boards of most Sydney’s high-fee private boys schools. Only two have attained gender equity. The culture of private boys schools has been put under the spotlight again after allegations that three Scots College students, all in their early teens, raped a girl in Bondi Junction. In a separate incident, three older teens – including two boys from St Gregory’s in Campbelltown – have been accused of raping a teenage girl. Related Article Opinion

Gender equality This Christian church has banned women elders. It’s a dangerous move Kylie Maddox Pidgeon Psychologist Gender diversity at the top filters down to the culture of the school. Female board representatives can help schools develop strong approaches to sexual consent education, to preparing boys for working alongside women as adults, and to navigating the horrendous social media algorithms to which many are exposed. Yet Sydney’s high-fee private boys schools have still struggled to achieve stronger female representation.



Some are hampered by tradition, others by rules. Their boards and councils are replete with old boys and male church members. That said, some schools cast off the old church governance and have switched to corporate-style boards to take control of assets and ensure they met governance standards. Kate Harper, an experienced consultant focusing on board search and leadership succession initiatives, said independent schools could look to the Australian Institute of Company Directors principles for not-for-profit boards. These recommend an appropriate mix of people with a diverse set of skills, experience and backgrounds that align with the organisation’s purpose, vision and strategy. “It is hard to see how a council dominated by one gender can effectively guide the school’s executive on preparing their students to deal with the many challenges and risks associated with social media, sexual consent, as well as preparation to join an increasingly gender-equal workforce,” she said. Many of Sydney’s high-fee private girls schools have reflected societal change and introduced equal gender or near-equal gender splits for board appointments. Boys’ schools must do the same.



The old-fashioned ideas that shaped these boys’ schools need a reboot. For the good of their students, the sector must embrace female leadership and relegate male bastion councils to the past. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: The bayside council, a missing recording, and closed-door vote notes
World.content:
NationalQueenslandPublic service The bayside council, a missing recording, and closed-door vote notes Matt Dennien August 24, 2026 — 7:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Welcome to Brisbane Times’ Queensland public sector column, Public Circus. This week: Right to Information answers (and questions) from the Redlands, how to move 584 boxes of sensitive docs, plum jobs from City Hall to 1WS, and more. A still-unresolved question hangs over the most senior appointed job on Brisbane’s bayside: what happened in the closed-doors meeting of Redland councillors on February 3 last year? After that meeting, then acting (now actual) chief executive Louise Rusan was parachuted in from outside the selection panel shortlist for council’s second crack at filling the $500,000 gig. Minutes from a contentious closed-door meeting of Redland City Council have been released to Brisbane Times under Right to Information laws. Good luck reading them. Michael Howard Thanks to the magic of Right to Information, we have some heavily redacted answers.



Council policy dictates that all so-called workshops and briefings are recorded – with that footage and an associated transcript held by the office of the chief executive. Circus used the information-release scheme to seek access to recordings and transcripts from that fateful meeting, and the follow-up a week later where Rusan fronted councillors. We were initially knocked back entirely by legal services manager Peter Cardiff because the 46 pages and one video found were deemed “not in the public interest” and would reveal personal information about candidates. (We explicitly said we weren’t fussed if those obviously sensitive details were withheld.) But wait – only one video for two meetings? We filed an internal review of the decision.



When that landed some time later, council’s principal audit and integrity services adviser Kailesh Naidu decided to release what were said to be “minutes taken by a council officer following the interviews of the unsuccessful CEO candidates”. This is despite the guidelines also dictating formal minutes are not to be taken. And while these were bizarrely redacted to withhold even councillor’s names, our news reporting on the issue helps fill in the black bars a touch. The minutes don’t seem to negate any of the concerns raised about how the closed-door vote departs from the public recruitment process, or if there was political interference.



(The council has repeatedly rejected such allegations, insisting proper processes were followed. We don’t suggest otherwise, only that questions have been raised internally and by external figures.) But we digress. Contained in the internal review decision was another detail: no recording is said to have been taken of the February 3 meeting “because all councillors and the mayor were present”. The guidelines certainly don’t place any such qualifications around the recording of the confidential meetings – though council backgrounding since has sought to suggest the guidelines didn’t apply to that type of meeting, and the notes weren’t formal minutes. So, what does the council formally have to say for itself? A spokesperson reiterated the process was consistent with local government laws.



“The appointment of the current CEO was a decision of Council in a General Meeting held on Wednesday 19 February 2025,” the spinner said in a written response to questions. Helpful. The recruitment matter is far from the only one being wrangled by the council at present, with leaks galore and mayor Jos Mitchell’s extended leave driving heated online debate among other councillors and political figures. A pointed submission by Cardiff on behalf of the council to the ongoing parliamentary inquiry into councillor conduct said the council had seen elected figures “avoid accountability” by being absent and suggested those on extended leave be subject to a misconduct probe. Police union and corruption watchdog discipline blue (again) goes public The regular appearances of state corruption watchdog figures before their parliamentary oversight committee are almost always worth a watch.



If not for some actual new information, then for the sport of MPs trying to goad Crime and Corruption Commission chair Bruce Barbour into revealing something about any of the agency’s tightly held probes into their political opponents. Queensland police union president Shane Prior and Crime and Corruption Commission chair Bruce Barbour have had at it in the paper. Catherine Strohfeldt / Dominic Lorrimer Last week, Barbour politely palmed questions around a handful of matters – think “Operation Cranberry” into the torpedoed recruitment of Krispin Hajkowicz as chief health officer, or former parole board president Michael Byrne’s alleged misuse of travel funds – into the private session of the hearing. Another element emerging from the committee session was a days-long subsequent public tit-for-tat between Barbour and police union president Shane Prior in the paper. Prior had taken umbrage with Barbour’s apparent “misleading” remarks about ongoing legal matters involving the watchdog’s disagreement with police about how it handles disciplinary matters where officers have unrecorded convictions.



Barbour has issued a rare public statement standing by his words. More detail emerged on Monday, when a watchdog spokesperson said three of the matters it had initiated in the Queensland Civil and Administrative Tribunal involved officers guilty of domestic violence offences who had not faced disciplinary action by police. How do you move 584 boxes of sensitive docs? Not in a ute – this time Another detail from the session also caught Circus’ eye: what was being done with 584 boxes of papers from the mothballed Connolly-Ryan inquiry into the CCC’s predecessor? Launched in 1996 by the fledgling Borbidge government, the inquiry was shut down by the Supreme Court a year later over a strong case of “ostensible bias” against its chair Peter Connolly.



Connolly had been accused of interfering with an independent probe being conducted for the then-Criminal Justice Commission into a memorandum of understanding between the police union and Coalition. So it is that the parliament – via the watchdog’s watchdog, Parliamentary Crime and Corruption Commissioner Dr Daniel Morgan – ended up lumped with the load of docs. Speaker of Queensland Parliament Pat Weir (centre) with Mitchell Kunde and Dr Daniel Morgan, in an image posted to announce the appointment of Morgan as the state’s Parliamentary Crime and Corruption Commissioner in June last year. Facebook / Pat Weir “Previously I think Mr [Mitchell] Kunde and somebody from the parliament used a ute to do it [move them],” Morgan said of the efforts from the commissioner’s longstanding principal legal officer to get the trove to a strongroom at the front of Old Parliament House. A document detailing a request to move them again (back in 2022) noted the records take up “six compactus bays and three locked storage cupboards” and would free up “many additional years’ worth of storage” if relocated.



And relocated they were due to be last Thursday morning. How? Circus feels Morgan’s description of last week’s plans is worth repeating in full. “Obviously, we were concerned to maintain the integrity of the documents. We literally cannot have them falling off the back of a truck. I made inquiries about an appropriate firm that had the necessary security experience and equipment. This firm has previously acted for the parliament and for the police. They are sensitive. They are not particularly highly secured documents, but we just need to know that the integrity is there that what has been packed is what has been delivered. We will be supervising that. I think we can ensure there will be locks on lots packed.” Parliamentary Crime and Corruption Commissioner Dr Daniel Morgan Quizzed by parliament’s crime and corruption committee chair, Ferny Grove Labor MP Mark Furner, about whether the papers were digitised, or whether the shift to the archives at Daisy Hill meant they would be, Morgan said there was “no further step intended”. Mermaid Beach LNP MP Ray Stevens then also jumped in, curious if this was out of cost concerns and seemingly confused as to why the boxes “which are not important apparently” are being retained but not digitised. In Morgan’s assessment, he didn’t see any benefit in this “apart from history”, with no one having sought access to them for some time. Kunde put this period at 15 years.



Morgan also noted the “special circumstances” around the inquiry and the subsequent custody of the related documents given to his office. Special circumstances indeed. And the kind that would probably make for some good (digitised) reading! Jobs, jobs and more jobs, from City Hall to the Tower of Power Readers looking for a change of scenery at work, look no further. This week has been a particularly lucrative one for job ads finding their way to the Circus tent. And what jobs they are. For the administratively minded, there’s an assistant ombudsman gig going over at the Queensland Ombudsman office, responsible for managing the team probing local government matters.



While reporting to the deputy ombudsman, who knows whether still-outgoing big boss Anthony Reilly’s boots will have been filled before applications close next Friday. Down at City Hall, the Olympic City council is apparently seeking to echo their Los Angeles counterparts by hiring an “international sports diplomacy project manager”. The headcount-happy Department of Premier and Cabinet are busy filling vacant roles – but what about the hiring squeeze? Matt Dennien That role will apparently be responsible for leading a related strategy, luring national Olympic and Paralympic committees, international federations and other groups to town and landing pre-Games training camps, global sporting partnerships and other related events. No pressure. The headcount-happy Department of Premier and Cabinet are also chasing an executive director of economic policy and director of communication, digital and design.



These last two raised our eyebrows given Crisafulli and Co’s keenness to put roadblocks in the way of new and even existing non-frontline roles. These ones? Vacancies for existing roles, a government flack tells us. Circus wonders what “vacancy management plan” hoops might exist at the top of the Tower of Power. Have a curiosity for the Circus tent? World.title: Swans staff give police statements as Heeney loses kids’ footy camp role
World.content:
Four Swans officials have given statements to police investigating an alleged sexual assault, as AFL boss Andrew Dillon banished the five suspended Sydney players from the Brownlow Medal count and confirmed the league would later conduct its own probe. The development came as one of the five players, Isaac Heeney, was dumped by a business he helped design that runs football camps for kids - 5th Quarter Camps. Sydney’s Isaac Heeney at last year’s Brownlow. He won’t be invited this year. AFL Photos “5th Quarter Camps is aware of a police investigation involving one of its shareholders, Isaac Heeney,” the business said in a statement to this masthead. “Although the investigation remains ongoing and no charges have been laid, given the circumstances and the seriousness of the matter, we can confirm Isaac Heeney will no longer have any involvement in 5th Quarter Camps.



“5th Quarter Camps takes seriously its responsibility to families, communities and commercial partners. We are committed to providing an environment founded on safety and respect, and doing everything in our power to ensure the wellbeing and experience of every child and family attending our camps remains at the centre of what we do.” The five Swans players suspended by Sydney for breaching the club’s behavioural standards are Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, Riley Bice and James Jordon. They were stood down for the remainder of the season after drinking, staying out late and inviting women back to the team hotel following their win over Essendon in round 23. Sydney Swans players (from left) James Jordon, Chad Warner, Isaac Heeney, Riley Bice and Nick Blakey have been suspended for the rest of the season. Nine The players’ club-imposed suspensions are separate from a Victoria Police investigation into an allegation of sexual assault in the early hours of last Monday morning at the Pullman East Melbourne hotel. No charges have been laid and a source with knowledge of the players’ position has said they deny criminal wrongdoing.



This masthead has previously reported that Heeney is a focus of the investigation. A source with knowledge of the police investigation, speaking anonymously, confirmed Sydney’s senior coach Dean Cox, football boss Leon Cameron, head of player wellbeing and development Brett Kirk and head of media and communications Tom Chadwick had given accounts to police. Callum Mills of the Swans embraces head coach Dean Cox after their game on Sunday. Getty Images The Swans declined to comment, citing the investigation. The four Sydney staff were not in the hotel room at Pullman East Melbourne when a woman alleges she was sexually assaulted.



Cameron, Kirk and Chadwick accompanied the five Swans players, who have since been handed club-imposed bans for the remainder of the season, in two cars as they drove home to Sydney from Melbourne last Monday afternoon. No Swans officials are accused of inappropriate behaviour and the club has previously said it had no issue with the conduct of Cox, who returned to the hotel not long after midnight. Andrew Dillon faces the media. AFL Photos via Getty Images At least two men aside from the five suspended players were in the hotel room on the night of the alleged sexual assault. This masthead revealed on Sunday that at least one fresh allegation of sexual assault and multiple claims of sexual conduct without consent had been made by the three women at the centre of the investigation.



It is not known which men the allegations are about, and to date police have only referenced “a report of a sexual assault”. This masthead is not suggesting any of the men in the room engaged in conduct of a sexual nature without consent, only that it has been alleged. Dillon said the AFL would not open its own investigation until the police probe was completed. “Those matters at the moment are under police investigation, so the AFL won’t be conducting any of its own inquiries until after the police investigation is finished,” he said. Loading “We don’t know where that will go and, at that stage, when that’s completed, the AFL will [undertake] some inquiries. I think what is clear is the Swans are taking action with the support of the AFL based on the information that is at hand now, and there’s been accountability for those players that were involved last week.”



The five players are still eligible to win the award for the AFL’s best and fairest player. Related Article Sydney Swans ‘Don’t abandon the club’: Swans fans ready to show support after week of turmoil “The invitations to the Brownlow will be going out this week. Those players won’t be invited,” Dillon said. “They are still eligible for the Brownlow but they’re under a club suspension, which goes until the end of the season.” Dillon said it was a matter for the Swans whether the players should still be allowed to win the club best and fairest. Dillon did not rule out the players being deregistered.



“Again, I’m not going to go into hypotheticals. We’ve got a police investigation that is underway. Once that’s completed, the AFL will make its own,” he said. Dillon said he was unaware if there was a recording of the alleged incident. “Look, I am not aware of that but, again, if there is a tape that’s relevant to the police investigation, it should be forwarded on to the police.” He denied the league had a wider cultural problem. “I think the actions of a few don’t take away from the thousands of people involved in football at all different levels who do great things all the time,” he said. “But what we do know is that we can do things better, and we’ll continue to do that, and we’ll continue to learn a bit better.”

World.title: CFMEU headquarters raided in secret-commissions probe
World.content:
Two senior CFMEU officials temporarily detained by Victoria Police’s Taskforce Hawk after detectives swooped on the union’s Victorian headquarters on Monday have dismissed allegations of union corruption or kickbacks involving the former boss of a bikie gang. The arrest and release of five serving CFMEU officials by Taskforce Hawk on Monday, with two facing minor charges, marks the most dramatic intervention yet by the elite police unit launched to tackle suspected crime and corruption in Victoria’s construction sector and which is now also gathering information for the upcoming royal commission. A Taskforce Hawk officer enters the CFMEU headquarters in Elizabeth Street in the CBD on Monday. Justin McManus The police action is a blow for the Albanese government-backed CFMEU administration two years into its attempt to reform the union, but it is not surprising given newly appointed administrator Michael Crosby’s recent concession that the scandal-tainted union had cleaned up in every jurisdiction except Victoria. In a statement released on Monday afternoon, Crosby confirmed that Hawk had “executed search warrants at six addresses, including CFMEU Victoria’s office, as part of an investigation into alleged secret commissions in the construction industry”.



“Criminals and bad actors in construction remain a major threat to the workers, which is why we need greater regulation and scrutiny across the sector,” Crosby said, warning that “anyone associated with criminal elements will have absolutely no place in this union’s future”. Police revealed homes in Chirnside Park, Westbury, Gisborne, Powelltown and Somerville were also searched on Monday. Investigators seized four CFMEU vehicles, 10 mobile phones, several laptops, documents, iPads, USBs, a .22 rifle and a prescription drug. The five men arrested were a 36-year-old from Chirnside Park, a 46-year-old from Westbury (near Moe), a 27-year-old from Gisborne, a 56-year-old from Powelltown and a 37-year-old from Somerville. A Chirnside Park man was charged with possessing a schedule 4 drug and bailed to appear at Ringwood Magistrates’ Court on November 10. A man from Westbury was charged with failing to store a long-arm firearm and ammunition as required. He was bailed to appear at Latrobe Valley Magistrates’ Court on January 11.



Three other men were released pending further inquiries. “The investigation relates to allegations of drug trafficking as well as secret commissions,” a police statement said. Crosby revealed he had ordered an internal investigation into the allegations, while also cautioning against rushing to judgment in respect of any of the officials arrested on Monday. “Taskforce Hawk has confirmed that to date no charges have been laid against any CFMEU official as part of this investigation. There is a presumption of innocence and the branch will continue to offer support whilst the investigation is ongoing,” he said. Also concerning for Crosby is the police decision to arrest one of his administration’s key reformers, Jason “Spike” Deans, a CFMEU official who multiple union and industry sources told The Age is respected as honest and hardworking.



Deans, the most senior of the union figures detained and released by Hawk, has stridently denied that the CFMEU has ever assisted the industrial relations business run by former Mongols bikie chief Tyrone “Little Ty” Bell. Deans, who was promoted to a key Victorian union leadership post just weeks ago by the CFMEU administration, told The Age he wanted to “make it very clear” that he and his fellow union official Matt Montebello had engaged in no impropriety in connection to Bell’s work as a union mediator. Montebello was also arrested and released without charge on Monday. “There has never been any untoward or any illegal activity from myself or Matt with … that little fella [Bell],” Deans said when contacted about the police inquiry when it was revealed by The Age last week.



“I’ve taken on this role because I care about good union members and their families. If anyone thinks that I’m here for the position or status they are very wrong. Matt Montebello was arrested as part of the raid on CFMEU headquarters on Monday. “I’m going to do what I need to do to get this union back into a functional position and I will make decisions that some people are not going to like. I will be ruthless to protect this union if I need to.” There is no suggestion by this masthead that Deans, Montebello or any of the other three officials arrested and released are engaged in any unlawful behaviour, only that police suspect they hold information relevant to their ongoing inquiry. When The Age contacted Montebello last week to ask him why he was a person of interest in Taskforce Hawk’s ongoing investigation into Bell and allegations the ex-bikie chief tried to influence the CFMEU, he also denied having any improper dealings with Bell.



“I’ve never taken a cent off him, mate,” Montebello said. Asked if he had ever discussed with Bell the CFMEU’s disruption of a Melbourne building project last September – the industrial dispute at the centre of the Hawk probe into Bell– Montebello denied any knowledge of the union action. “Don’t know what you’re talking about, mate,” he said, before hanging up. Last Thursday, The Age revealed that Bell, a former national vice-president of the Mongols outlaw bikie gang, was being probed by police over allegations he offered inducements to officials still serving in the CFMEU in return for their support of his business, Dynamis HSR. The Age also revealed that the Taskforce Hawk operation that led to Monday’s arrests and a raid of the CFMEU’s Swanston Street headquarters was examining whether CFMEU organisers leaked Bell information or co-ordinated union activity with him in order to advance the interests of Bell’s industrial relations consultancy.



Bell’s connections to the CFMEU were cultivated via two channels: his relatively brief stint as a CFMEU delegate working for building company Markscon, and his long-standing social and schooling ties to serving and ex-CFMEU organisers and delegates, including Montebello and his brother Kane Montebello, a high-ranking Hells Angels member who also served as a union delegate. Three CFMEU sources said the administration had sought and received reassurance from Matt Montebello that he had cut ties or was carefully managing his familial relationships with people linked to outlaw motorcycle gangs. Related Article Exclusive

Building Bad Ex-bikie boss under investigation over alleged inducements to CFMEU officials In addition to his brother, Montebello’s cousin has also held a role with the Hells Angels and was briefly recruited into the union. An undated photo circulating in the construction industry, but which appears to be several years old, shows Montebello wearing a Hells Angels support singlet. There is no suggestion he has ever held a role in the club or been involved in bikie activity.



Montebello’s brother, cousin and Bell were among the highest-profile serving and ex-bikie gang members recruited into the CFMEU between 2021 and 2024, only to be forced out in July 2024 when this masthead’s Building Bad series first broke. Last week, Bell described the police allegations as “just ridiculous” and defended Matt Montebello. “I’ve been friends with him since primary school, and his brother and I feel very sorry for the guy, because he loves his job,” Bell said. “I hope you don’t write anything bad about that guy, because he’s a very good dad, a very good person,” he said. CFMEU assistant administrator Matt McGowan said: “CFMEU has been made aware of a police operation this morning as part of Taskforce Hawk. As this is a live police matter, CFMEU cannot comment further at this time.” Get the day’s breaking news, entertainment ideas and a long read to enjoy. World.title: How a personal pitch from the PNG prime minister helped seal Manu’s NRL return
World.content:
Updated SportNRLNRL 2026 How a personal pitch from the PNG prime minister helped seal Manu’s NRL return Dan Walsh Updated August 24, 2026 — 9:30pm ,first published August 24, 2026 — 7:32am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A personal sales pitch from Papua New Guinea Prime Minister James Marape helped seal Joey Manu’s return to rugby league, which is expected to begin with a short-term 2027 deal at an NRL rival before he takes up a two-year deal with the PNG Chiefs from 2028. The Kiwi international’s long-touted signing with the expansion franchise was confirmed on Monday morning. Loading Manu has already been offered to several NRL clubs as a potential short-term signing for the back half of 2027 once he completes the final year of his estimated €1 million ($1.6 million) contract with French rugby outfit Racing 92. He will be 31 by the time he links with PNG for their first pre-season late next year, and the Chiefs can see an advantage in Manu joining an NRL rival as a pre-June 30 signing, as was raised by the Warriors earlier this season.



Manu ultimately knocked back that approach to ensure he didn’t jeopardise his lucrative rugby deal. But his appeal and pedigree as a potential game-breaker in next year’s title race have been noted at several clubs spoken to by this masthead on Monday after his PNG move was announced. A $300,000 sign-on figure for a three-month return was reported earlier this year as a fair market value, according to the NRL salary cap auditor for the Kiwi star; it would equate to a $1.2 million salary. Former Rooster Joey Manu and his family – pictured at Port Moresby airport – toured the Chiefs facilities earlier this year. His signature comes as the Chiefs continue to reshape a volatile player market, with Hudson Young to begin formal talks with PNG next month despite Canberra tabling him a record $3.3 million, three-year extension offer – the richest deal in the club’s history. The Chiefs are also in talks with Titans star AJ Brimson after he was given permission to explore an early exit from the Gold Coast.



Speaking from France after committing to PNG as their seventh signing, Manu said Marape’s passion for bringing an NRL side to the wider Pacific region had helped sway him, while he had also been impressed by the Chiefs’ Port Moresby facilities. “Talking to the [PNG] prime minister, how passionate he was about making it not just a Papua New Guinea team but making it a Pacific team, and trying to get the Pacific nations behind this team, I think it’s going to be special,” Manu said. Joey Manu left the NRL as one of the best players in the game. NRL Imagery “I’m a really proud Cook Island and Māori man, and I know my family’s real proud back in Tokoroa in New Zealand – and also in the Cook Islands, too. “There’s so much talent in the Pacific Islands and rugby league is taking over the islands, so it’s really cool to have sort of a Pacific team.”



The Australian government’s much-discussed $600 million funding package around the club sets aside as much as $350 million in rugby league pathways development programs across PNG, Fiji, Samoa and Tonga, according to a Senate estimates committee hearing held last year. Related Article Analysis

NRL 2026 Good luck, NRL rivals. The Warriors can now stay in NZ until grand final week Manu looms as a potential fullback option given he regularly wore the No.1 for New Zealand at Test level. A rugby league return at centre – where he was widely regarded as the best in the game throughout a 181-game career with the Roosters – may be more suitable, though, given his age and the added running required of fullbacks under the NRL’s new set-restart rules. “It’s just been a few years now since I’ve been out of the game, and I still watch a few games when I can,” Manu said.



“You miss certain things when you’re watching, and I’m just grateful that I get to come back and play. Rugby league is a special game for myself and to come back and play in the NRL is very special.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: A piece o’ cord for bouncers
World.content:
“Adding to the ridiculous practice of establishments requiring a tie for entry (C8), in the late ’60s I was denied entry to the Chatswood Charles Hotel. They stated I needed a tie,” says Max Redmayne of Drummoyne. “My response was to take a shoelace and create a bow tie, and yes, that was acceptable, which points to the ludicrous practice.”

“During the 1997 Australian Professional Sumo Tour I was deputised by Wide World of Sports to take two sumo wrestlers to Eagle Farm racecourse for a day out and to present the trophy for the main race,” writes Katrina Watts of Murwillumbah. “They wore traditional cotton yukata (kimono) and zori (straw sandals). As they were greeted and ushered into the members enclosure I heard a dapper gent comment, ‘Just a minute, those two men can’t come in here. They are in dresses, have no ties and are wearing thongs!’”

Of course there are some establishments that secede from a typical dress code, as evidenced by Denis O’Calahan of Auckland, New Zealand: “In 1976, I was in Dallas, Texas, for training. They took us out to a restaurant called The Traildust where the sign on the door said ‘No Neckties’. If anyone tried to enter wearing a tie, a waiter would come out with a huge pair of scissors and cut it off. The walls were decorated with hundreds of the cut-off ties.”

James White of Beverage (Vic) reckons the media have blown the gig: “Whose cage do I rattle to get the news out that last weekend, Boyd Excell won his eighth consecutive title at the Four-in-Hand World Championship in Europe? He is a spectacular competitor in a sport that is spectacular But nothing in the news.”

“In the early 1970s, I was refused admission to Eastern Suburbs Leagues Club due to my hair being over my collar,” recalls Geoff Genford of Hurlstone Park.“I didn’t feel so bad when I read that hirsute star player and former rugby union international Russell Fairfax was taken into the club to sign his contract via the tradesman’s entrance.” Margaret Bellingham Holle of Woollahra remembers it, too.

World.title: ‘Could see myself sitting here’: One Nation MP Farley gatecrashes Liberal meeting
World.content:
One Nation MP David Farley has fuelled speculation about his future in Pauline Hanson’s party after accidentally walking into a private meeting of more than 20 Liberal MPs – then telling them he could see himself sitting with them. The extraordinary encounter happened in Parliament House last Wednesday when Farley wandered into a regular meeting of Liberal MPs from marginal seats. Several Liberals present said the Farrer MP took a while to realise he was in the wrong room before turning to leave. Farrer MP David Farley during his swearing-in on June 2. Alex Ellinghausen “I could see myself sitting here,” Farley told the MPs, before walking out. “We were all taken aback, to be honest,” one Liberal MP said. “It was a very loose thing to say.”



Farley confirmed the incident on Monday, but portrayed it as an off-the-cuff joke after accidentally entering the room. Editor's pick Immigration Every morning, a grandmother wakes 11 children. Their parents are thousands of kilometres away He said the Liberal MPs had a “who-hit-John” look on their faces, silent with their mouths open, before he “filled the empty space with my quip” and left. Liberal MP Andrew Hastie said Farley was currently a member of One Nation “but certainly let’s see what the future holds”. “He’s a decent fellow, I’ve met him a couple of times,” Hastie told ABC’s 7.30.



The remark comes at an awkward time for One Nation, with Farley again publicly at odds with Hanson over one of the party’s central political issues. The Farrer MP told ABC’s Insiders that while One Nation wanted to reduce net overseas migration to 130,000, it would allow another 100,000 migrant workers through skilled visas, backpacker programs and the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility scheme. That would put the effective number at about 230,000 – broadly in line with Labor’s forecast of 225,000 by 2027–28. Hanson moved quickly to reject Farley’s interpretation, insisting One Nation’s policy was to cut net overseas migration to 130,000, with some short-term agricultural workers excluded from the official measure. One Nation leader Pauline Hanson and Farley, pictured on May 13, don’t see eye to eye on the party’s net overseas migration figure. Alex Ellinghausen



One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce was then sent out to clean up the mess, telling Sunrise that Farley had simply got it wrong. “Show me a political career where people haven’t made a mistake, and I’ll show you a person who’s not told the truth.” Joyce said One Nation had seemingly raised the matter with Farley but refused to elaborate. “Oh, look, I’m not going to throw anybody under a bus,” he said. “When people are new in parliament, they can sometimes get things incorrect, and that’s what happens. God knows I’ve done it enough.” “I think [Farley] would have been offended by [One Nation’s head of operations] James Ashby going on News24 last night with a mop and essentially mocking what I thought were his thoughtful contributions on [ABC’s] Insiders yesterday,” Hastie said.



Hastie was referring to Ashby’s appearance on News24 on Sunday night where he brandished a mop and clarified One Nation’s migration policies, stating he’d spoken to Farley and that “people make mistakes”. “For a new member of parliament, it’s always difficult getting your head around those [net overseas migration] numbers,” Ashby said. Farley’s comments were also savaged by online news site One News Australia, which branded his appearance a “rookie blunder” and claimed his “clueless” performance had given Labor an “escape route” from its migration policy. The criticism is notable given One News Australia’s origins as the One Nation Supporters Network before it was rebranded as a news organisation. The site and the party say they have no affiliation, although its coverage is strongly pro-One Nation and Hanson. Farley was previously counselled by Hanson during the Farrer byelection campaign after he agreed a net migration figure of 306,000 last year was “probably not” too many.



The pair also exchanged harsh words after it was revealed that he’d previously tried to seek preselection with Labor for the seat and not informed anyone within One Nation before it was revealed by this masthead. Related Article Immigration Pauline Hanson’s deleted post deepens One Nation’s migration muddle Farley has already shown he is prepared to depart from Hanson’s position in the parliament. Last week he voted with the Coalition on an amendment to Labor’s wagering legislation, despite Hanson having previously committed to supporting the government’s ban on foreign matched lotteries. His growing independence is being watched closely by Coalition MPs, particularly given his conservative and agricultural background.



Sources in the Coalition said Opposition Leader Angus Taylor knew Farley from his time as an agribusiness leader and could potentially use the relationship to court him in future, although there are no immediate plans to do so. “He is a Nat or a country Liberal, not a populist,” one Liberal MP said. Farley told Insiders he came from the conservative LNP tradition, joined the Nationals after returning to Farrer and later explored joining Labor and running as an independent. He ultimately chose One Nation because he said it offered the “political courage” and “tenacity” he wanted. “I have the full support of the party to pursue what I’m doing, especially for Farrer,” he said.
